fullText:
BENGALURU, India (AP) — This year's powerful El Nino and the record global heat it's driving, along with severe droughts, wildfires and shrinking water supplies, could lead to nearly half a million more deaths worldwide by the end of February, according to a research report released Wednesday.

The grim warning by the University of Chicago-based Climate Impact Lab says that as many as 451,000 more heat-related deaths between June and the end of February could be attributed to El Nino, compared with heat deaths expected in a typical year.

The heaviest toll, the group says, is expected in poorer countries, already struggling with food insecurity and high energy costs, partly due to climate change and the fallout of the war in Iran.

Michael Greenstone, a co-founder of the group and the study's co-author, said the heat danger will likely persist beyond February — even though this El Nino is expected to end by then. The fallout of the weather phenomenon could be felt well into next summer, he added.

The research, he said, shows that heat is most dangerous in places that are already hot and relatively poor.

"If you're already in a hot place, the extra couple of degrees are going to be much more dangerous," he said. Wealthier places, he added, generally have greater access to air conditioning, reliable water supplies and functioning health systems.

The study combined seasonal temperature forecasts with localized estimates of how high temperatures affect mortality across more than 24,000 regions worldwide.

Researchers estimated the additional heat-related deaths by comparing deaths expected under El Nino-driven high temperatures with deaths expected if temperatures remained similar to what they have been in the last three decades. The projected fatalities are for the entire El Nino period, from June 2026 until the end of February 2027.

The study by Greenstone and his colleagues also warns that the Global South — a term that isn't geographical but a reference to developing countries in general — will bear the heaviest burden of the excessive heat.

The researchers behind the report found that the Sahel region in Africa — countries along the semiarid southern fringe of the Sahara Desert — is expected to be the hardest-hit, with about 66,800 additional deaths caused by El Nino-driven heat.

Other major hot spots include South and Southeast Asia and parts of Latin America, according to the report. The researchers project about 19,400 additional heat-related deaths across the Philippines, Vietnam, Thailand and Cambodia, as well as 19,300 in Indonesia, 15,800 in India and 13,300 in Brazil.

With such staggering numbers, there are recommended measures that governments can take, the report says. They include heat-warning systems, cooling centers, hydration stations, protections for outdoor workers, expanded hospital capacity and targeted outreach to elderly people and other vulnerable groups.

The authors also call for what they describe as anticipatory financing, so governments can move resources before dangerous heat peaks.

Abhiyant Tiwari, a heat expert at NRDC India who was not involved in the study, said the report's projections should serve as a call to action rather than be another reason for alarm.

But while it's one thing to have well thought-out plans — as India does — implementing these plans and raising needed funds remains a challenge, he said.

"The real measure of our preparedness is not how many heat warnings we issue, but how effectively we protect people and reduce preventable deaths," Tiwari added.

El Nino is a natural climate pattern, but this year's unusually strong event is occurring on a planet already warmed by human-caused climate change, increasing the risks from extreme heat.

The Climate Impact Lab said global land temperatures during this El Nino could be higher by about 1.2 Celsius (2.1 Fahrenheit), producing 44% more extremely hot days than in a typical year. The report said those temperature increases may mirror conditions that climate change could make common some 20 years from now.

That's why this El Nino could offer a preview of what's ahead as the planet continues to warm, the report said. It's also an opportunity for decision-makers "to see exactly where emergency actions can be taken now to save tens of thousands of lives," the authors say.

title: Supreme Court stays out of custody dispute between California couple and surrogate
description:
Washington —  The Supreme Court on Tuesday declined to intervene in a custody dispute between a California couple and surrogate who gave birth to a child last month with a rare and serious heart defect.
Justice Elena Kagan rejected the emergency appeal from the woman, McKenna West, who had asked the justices to halt a California court order declaring the couple, Omar Ahmed and Nausheen Gilkar, to be the child's parents.
Kagan handles emergency appeals arising from California and other states in the region.
The legal battle involves a surrogacy contract Gilkar and Ahmed entered into with West, which allowed the couple to demand an abortion for a baby diagnosed with a fetal abnormality, according to court filings.
West, who lives in Alaska, became pregnant with a baby boy in December.

title: Hurricane Polo explodes into one of Pacific's strongest ever — but landfall isn't forecast
description:
Hurricane Polo has exploded into a monstrous Category 5 storm with 180-mph winds, becoming the second-strongest hurricane ever recorded in the eastern Pacific as it threatens Mexico’s southwestern coast with life-threatening floods and mudslides.
The National Hurricane Center said Polo was still strengthening after rapidly intensifying on Tuesday. The storm is expected to remain “extremely dangerous” for the next several days as it tracks northwestward over an ocean environment loaded with extremely warm water, abundant moisture and low wind shear.
“Therefore even more strengthening is possible,” the hurricane center warned, raising the prospect of an even more powerful storm as Polo continues feeding on the overheated Pacific.
Hurricane Polo threatens flash floods and mudslides.

description:

fullText:
UNITED NATIONS/DUBAI, Sept 23 (Reuters) - Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian said in a speech at the UN on Wednesday that Tehran would never surrender to the US but still believes in diplomacy, a day after President Donald Trump used the same forum to threaten to "annihilate" Iran.

The duelling speeches at the ‌annual UN General Assembly in New York bookended the first shuttle talks between the United States and Iran for months, which appeared to have yielded no concessions in the public ‌stance of either side towards ending the Middle East war.

In his speech, Pezeshkian defended Iran's military actions as defensive, and insisted Iran was not seeking nuclear weapons.

In a potential new flashpoint, Iran also threatened to act against its neighbours if they ​abide by new US sanctions intended to ground Iranian civilian aircraft worldwide.

Washington has said it will impose so-called secondary sanctions against any country that allows Iranian flights after Wednesday. Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council, told state TV Iran would ensure neighbouring countries' airports could not function if they stop Iranian flights.

The annual UN gathering in New York provided the occasion on Tuesday for Iranian and U.S. officials to hold their first known indirect talks since a ceasefire collapsed in July, with Iran's Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi and US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner communicating through mediators on the sidelines.

"Steve and Jared had a ‌very productive meeting today with mediators of Iran," Trump said on Tuesday ⁠after his own speech. "I think there's a lot of momentum for them to make a deal. It's what we're hearing from everybody."

Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmail Baghaei said Tehran had engaged with Washington through a Qatari mediator and conveyed conditions, including an end to the war on all fronts and a halt to ⁠US "acts of aggression".

Some Iranian state media initially reported that Araqchi and Witkoff had met, but Iranian officials clarified to Reuters that it was not face-to-face.

IRAN HARDLINERS RESIST DIPLOMATIC MOVES

The diplomatic contact in New York caused a backlash in Iranian media associated with hardliners.

An opinion piece run by the semi-official Tasnim news agency, associated with the Revolutionary Guards, said Araqchi was wrong to have contacts with Witkoff and Kushner, "a major gift to Trump", as Iran had ​already ​conveyed its terms.

Iranian sources told Reuters the delegation had been ordered not to meet the Americans face-to-face by the ​Supreme National Security Council, a body that includes figures selected by Ayatollah Mojtaba ‌Khamenei, the supreme leader. Khamenei has yet to appear in public since replacing his father, who was killed on the war's first day.

One Iranian journalist covering the visit told Reuters that some hardliners viewed the trip to New York itself as an insult to the memory of the slain leader, Ali Khamenei.

OIL PRICES HOLD NEAR TWO-WEEK LOW

Still, the diplomatic opening helped keep oil prices near two-week lows. Brent crude hovered around $100 a barrel after surging earlier this month when Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis launched a major offensive, threatening traffic through the Red Sea, an alternative Saudi export route.

The war, launched by Trump in February alongside Israel as "Operation Epic Fury", has lasted nearly seven months, killing thousands of people, disrupting global energy supplies and spreading to other countries in the region — particularly to Lebanon and more recently to Yemen.

An ‌interim agreement reached in June, signed by Trump and Pezeshkian, would have given Iran its main demands: lifting financial ​sanctions and unfreezing assets in return for talks on limiting its nuclear programme.

But that deal unravelled within weeks over shipping ​rules in the Strait of Hormuz, conduit for a fifth of global oil and liquefied ​natural gas before the war. Iran wants to exert control and collect fees from ships that use it, which Washington rejects.

In the latest reported attack in the ‌strait, Britain's UKMTO maritime security agency said a cargo ship had been hit ​by projectiles, causing two casualties among the crew. ​The crew had been evacuated and the ship was on fire and adrift.

Despite near-daily attacks, traffic through the strait has picked up in recent weeks. Oil producers pay shipping companies fees of as much as a quarter of a cargo's value to take the wartime risk of sailing through the strait with transponders switched off, before transferring crude to other vessels on ​the far side.

Exports from the United Arab Emirates have already recovered to ‌pre-war levels, and Saudi Arabia has sold 60 million barrels of Gulf oil for both this month and next, to be delivered beyond the strait off the coast of ​Oman.

Nevertheless, a third of Gulf oil is estimated to be missing from global supplies. Shortages have particularly hit refined products such as diesel, causing inflation, pushing up interest ​rates and hurting Trump's Republicans.

Trump Hails 'Very Good' Iran Talks Following Annihilation Threat

The GOP backlash, which has been simmering below the surface throughout Trump's second term as lawmakers privately grumbled he hasn't focused enough on affordability issues, burst into public view as a rapid succession of Republicans challenged Trump on everything from the Iran war to the president's "lavish" summit this week with Chinese President Xi Jinping.

Republicans have long been loathe to openly criticize the president, who has wielded an uncommonly strong hold over his party and retains long memories about who has crossed him. Back in May, eight Indiana state lawmakers who defied Trump on a redistricting plan faced their primary voters, and only two won. The president that month similarly ended Texas Senator John Cornyn's political career by backing Ken Paxton's primary challenge instead.

So confident is the president of his singular electoral magnetism that his rallying cry at campaign events from Texas to North Carolina has been to call on his supporters to vote as if he's on the ballot in November.

Yet those same Republican lawmakers who held tight with Trump through the primaries are now facing a general election environment and a very different electorate. They now have to contend not just with GOP voters, but Democrats who've always opposed the president, as well as disaffected independents who've drifted from Trump over economic concerns.

Retail gasoline prices are up. So is diesel. The cost of financing government debt has risen since the Iran war began, driving up the cost of mortgages, credit cards and consumer debt. And a confident White House that has unapologetically pursued all of its priorities at once, from tariffs to getting Trump's name on the Kennedy Center, is increasingly seen as unfocused on the costs Americans pay to go about their daily lives.

Trump's reservoir of support began to crack last week, when Florida Republican Maria Elvira Salazar cut a video telling Trump that his immigration crackdowns have gone "too far," as she battles to retain her House seat in a Miami-area district heavily impacted by the administration's deportation policies.

title: Hegseth impeachment fight could put Democrats in a bind after the midterms
description:
The impeachment effort against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth posed a dilemma for Republican leaders ahead of the midterms. In the lame duck, it could be Democrats in the bind.
Hegseth is leading an unpopular war in Iran, and GOP leaders were eager to avoid an impeachment vote this month, which would have put some vulnerable Republicans in a tough spot heading into November’s elections. Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) defused the issue by punting that vote until after the elections.
fullText:
The impeachment effort against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth posed a dilemma for Republican leaders ahead of the midterms. In the lame duck, it could be Democrats in the bind.

Hegseth is leading an unpopular war in Iran, and GOP leaders were eager to avoid an impeachment vote this month, which would have put some vulnerable Republicans in a tough spot heading into November’s elections. Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) defused the issue by punting that vote until after the elections.

But the tides are likely to turn after the election, when Republicans will be freed to weigh in on Hegseth’s fate without fear of a voter backlash, while Democrats will face a tougher choice.

Do they go charging after Hegseth full bore, to appease a liberal base demanding Pentagon accountability? Or do they tread more cautiously, to allow time for the formal investigations many Democrats say they want to see before backing something as explosive as impeachment?

Rep. Jamie Raskin (Md.), the senior Democrat on the House Judiciary Committee, which has jurisdiction over impeachment proceedings, suggested that answering those questions won’t be easy.

“I think that all impeachment articles should be sent to the Judiciary Committee, and we should scrutinize them,” Raskin, a former professor of constitutional law, said last week as Congress was leaving Washington for the long campaign recess.

“I’m not a huge fan of pop-up impeachments,” Raskin continued, “but if that’s all Speaker Johnson leaves us, then we will have to take it very seriously.”

The issue will be an early, postelection test for House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.), who has walked a delicate line under President Trump’s second term as he vies to become the first Black Speaker in U.S. history.

On one hand, Jeffries has faced pressure from the left to fight the president tooth and nail at every turn, no matter the topic. On the other, Jeffries has sought to avoid alienating more moderate voters who are the key to winning battleground districts.

His decision will become even trickier if Democrats flip control of the House, because Jeffries’s ascension to the Speakership will hinge on his ability to win 218 votes on the floor in the first week of January. That task will require the support of all Democrats, from battleground centrists who are cold to aggressive impeachments, to incoming democratic socialists who might view the vote on Hegseth’s removal as a gauge of Jeffries’s leadership credentials.

Jeffries has taken pains to balance those pressures by attacking Hegseth’s track record and calling for his firing while refusing to say if he’ll support impeachment.

“We haven’t ruled anything out when it comes to all of the tools available to us to hold people accountable, and we haven’t ruled anything in. That’s been our position. That will remain our position,” Jeffries told reporters in the Capitol last week.

“Pete Hegseth should’ve never been confirmed. This guy is the most unqualified so-called secretary of war in American history,” he added. “He’s the architect of Operation Epic Failure in Iran that has increased gas prices on everyday Americans and further burdened them economically. … It’s my view that’s the reason why [GOP leaders] pulled the resolution, because there were Republicans who can’t even defend Pete Hegseth at this point.”

The resolution in question, sponsored by Rep. Thomas Massie (R-Ky.), features eight articles of impeachment accusing Hegseth of abuses of power related to his handling of the Iran war, a failure to protect civilians and the extrajudicial killings of alleged drug smugglers in international waters, among other charges. Massie introduced the proposal as a privileged resolution, which forces a floor vote even over the objections of GOP leaders.

Johnson evaded that vote by cutting the House calendar a day short last week. But the clock resumes when the House returns on Nov. 9, making Hegseth’s impeachment a first order of business in the lame-duck session.

Democrats have seized on Johnson’s decision, saying Republicans simply feared taking a tough vote ahead of the midterms — an attack that’s allowed them to highlight the unpopular Iran war.

“You talk to Republicans here — which I do a lot, because I’m on the Armed Services and Intel committee — a vast majority of people do not like Pete Hegseth. They think he’s incompetent, at best. They think he’s a clown and a joker at worst. … And a lot of people are somewhere in between,” said Rep. Jason Crow (D-Colo.). “They don’t want to vote on it.”

Johnson has rejected that narrative as “ridiculous,” saying he simply wanted to grant lawmakers more time to campaign.

But attacking Johnson over the process is different from throwing your weight behind impeachment. Even after the vote was delayed, Democratic leaders distanced themselves from Massie’s resolution and promoted a more deliberative process.

“The DOD mismanagement is incredibly clear, but let’s be honest. The only calls, the only discussions about impeachment in the halls of Congress this week have been from Republicans to impeach Pete Hegseth. No Democratic members were making those calls,” said Rep. Pete Aguilar (Calif.), the chair of the House Democratic Caucus.

“We believe in oversight and accountability — that is a hallmark of what this chamber should be doing,” he continued. “We will do that job. We will do it in a thoughtful way.”

Aguilar’s remarks ignored another impeachment push just before the recess, when Democratic Rep. Al Green (Texas) forced a vote to remove Trump over the killing of several civilians by immigration enforcement officers. Many Democrats were furious with Green for distracting from the party’s economic message, and every member of leadership sought to balance competing internal interests by voting “present” — a strategy that could forecast how they’ll approach the Hegseth resolution.

However, heading into that vote, at least one powerful Democrat said Massie has made “very compelling” points about the laws of war and the possibility that Hegseth violated them, which could make it tough for Democrats to do anything but support impeachment.

“He raises a bunch of profound arguments,” Raskin said, “and I’m taking it extremely seriously.”

title: Wales suffer scrum-half Lockwood blow for USA Test
description: Scrum-half Seren Lockwood is out of Wales' second WXV Test, against USA, after failing a head injury assessment.
fullText:
Scrum-half Seren Lockwood has been ruled out of Wales' second WXV Global Series fixture, against USA in Cardiff on Saturday, after failing a head injury assessment.

Lockwood was taken off during the first half of Wales' eight-try victory over South Africa and is now going through World Rugby's return to play protocols.

It is a blow for Wales with Lockwood and Keira Bevan proving a promising half-back partnership in a new-look backline.

Her absence paves the way for Lleucu George to return at 10, with Bevan reverting to her usual position of nine at Cardiff Arms Park.

"It's always sad to see an individual coming off, but the HIA is great to have on board, we're looking after her," said Wales head coach Sean Lynn.

"She's not going to be available this weekend, but I'm super excited to see the half-back combination that we've got this week."

Wales deliver performance of serious promise

Inspired Wales seal stunning win over South Africa

Carys Cox's return to fitness after summer knee surgery gives Lynn another option in the backline, with Cox able to play centre and on the wing.

"Carys has been superb in rehab, she feels fitter, faster and stronger," said Lynn.

"She always brings a smile, she's always confident and I love her athleticism. She will always beat that first defender and the way we are playing now, she's going to get some ball in hand."

Saturday's game at Cardiff Arms Park comes too soon for fellow back Nel Metcalfe, who will not be ready until next month's two-Test tour of Japan.

"Nel is progressing really well with her rehab, we saw her today in some rugby elements, so fingers crossed we will be seeing her in Japan," Lynn added.

title: Yu, 13, completes hat-trick of golds at Asian Games
description: Thirteen-year-old swimming star Yu Zidi claims a dominant victory in the 400m individual medley to complete a hat-trick of gold medals at the Asian Games.
fullText:
Thirteen-year-old swimming star Yu Zidi claimed a dominant victory in the 400m individual medley to complete a hat-trick of gold medals at the Asian Games.

China's Yu led from start to finish as she set a new Games record of four minutes 28.56 seconds, smashing the previous record - which had stood since 2014 - by nearly 4.5 seconds.

Her time is the fourth fastest in the world this year, with only Canada's world record holder Summer McIntosh having gone quicker.

Yu was 3.95 seconds clear of compatriot Ke Wenxi, who took silver, with Japan's Mio Narita claiming bronze.

Having already won gold in the 200m butterfly and 200m individual medley in Nagoya - both in Games record times - Yu is being widely tipped to contend for the medals at the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics.

Meanwhile, North Korea weightlifter Ri Song Gum broke three world records on her way to securing her third Asian Games gold in the women's 49kg category.

Defending champion Ri, 28, lifted 94kg in the snatch segment and followed up with a clean-and-jerk of 121kg, both marks 1kg more than the previous world bests.

It gave her a total haul of 215kg - some 4kg more than the previous world record.

"The world record and this gold medal hold great meaning for me, because of everything I poured into this competition," Ri said.

"I stepped out on to the competition floor today carrying that faith and those expectations."

title: Pocognoli has 'positive nervousness' for Scotland debut
description: Scotland head coach Sebastien Pocognoli admits to feeling a "positive nervousness" before his first game in charge of the country, a Nations League tie against Slovenia in Ljubljana on Saturday.
fullText:
Nations League: Slovenia v Scotland

Saturday 26 September, 14:00 BST

Scotland head coach Sebastien Pocognoli admits to feeling a "positive nervousness" before his first game in charge of the country, a Nations League tie against Slovenia in Ljubljana on Saturday.

The Belgian was appointed in August, replacing Steve Clarke, whose seven-year tenure ended after Scotland's exit at the group stages of the World Cup.

Pocognoli starts with four Nations League matches across 11 days, with the trip to Slovenia followed by Switzerland at Hampden, a fixture in North Macedonia, then a return meeting with the Slovenes in Glasgow.

"If we talk about nerves, yes, but it's a positive nervousness," he told BBC Sport Scotland. "We have a job with responsibility. It's excitement and I'm just passionate about being on the touchline."

Scotland are currently at a warm weather camp in La Manga, Spain with a much-changed squad.

Pocognoli has picked a 19-year-old in James Wilson, four 20-year-olds - Findlay Curtis, Ben Gannon-Doak, Lennon Miller and Colby Donovan - and another three aged 22 - Kristi Montgomery, Luke Graham and Robbie Ure.

With Blackburn's Montgomery replacing the injured Kenny McLean, there are now eight uncapped players in the squad.

"It's a lot of new faces, so it's a challenge to find the right balance, to keep the cohesion in the team," Pocognoli said.

Well-travelled Binks eager to make mark for Scotland

From leaving Rangers to La Liga - Scotland is next step for Ure

McPake's 'colourful' journey from club-less to Scotland call-up in three years

The manager says he knows his team and his formation for the Slovenia game but is not wedded to any particular system, although playing three at the back has been a staple of his coaching to this point.

"I always think the players select themselves," he added. "We have four games, so we need to plan. We need to have a periodisation [managing training loads, games and recovery] about the tactical aspect and the physical aspect.

"This team can be flexible. We're ready for the four games in terms of what kind of approach we want to give."

Pocognoli revealed he has had a conversation with his predecessor, Clarke - "a nice meeting on the phone," as he put it.

"He was very kind, very... humble. That was very helpful for me. It just was to let me know that he's behind the team. He was very happy [in his time in the job] but he also felt that it was the right time [to leave]. He wished me all the best.

"I will try to be as successful as the previous staff because we want to play in a big tournament. We want to create this moment for the country."

Asked if his brand of football will involve more risk and adventure than Clarke's, he said: "We have to find the right balance because if you play fantastic football and you don't qualify you get some criticism."

Pocognoli's style is all about aggressive pressing and fast tempo. He says that it might take a while for cohesion to be achieved but there are certain things that he wants to see straight away against Slovenia.

"For me, it's about the personality of the players," he added. "I like a unit team who are just fighting for each other.

"It's a basic principle - attack together and squeeze the pitch. When we need to defend, it's just to defend like brothers. When we lose the ball, it's try to regain the ball as quickly as possible.

"From that, there are a lot of other principles, but that's the base. If you cannot get this, you will never have good principles on the pitch."

Given the condensed nature of the games, there is going to be a fair degree of rotation from Slovenia away, to Switzerland at home, to North Macedonia away and Slovenia at home.

"So good so far," Pocognoli said about what he has seen in La Manga. "But we need to get the response through the games. It's up to them to perform well, but it's up to me to make them perform well."

Fight for each other and defend like brothers - Pocognoli's Scotland blueprint

title: 'It can't be brushed over' - Republic of Ireland squad to discuss Israel games
description: Dara O'Shea says the Republic of Ireland squad will wait until after Thursday's Kosovo game before discussing how they approach Sunday's contentious fixture against Israel.
fullText:
Dara O'Shea says the Republic of Ireland squad will wait until after Thursday's Kosovo game before discussing how they approach Sunday's contentious fixture against Israel.

The Republic of Ireland face Kosovo in Pristina on Thursday (19:45 BST) before travelling to Debrecen in Hungary for the first of two Israel games in this international window.

There have been increasing calls in Ireland for a boycott of the matches, with a protest held at the Republic of Ireland team hotel in Dublin on Monday.

This followed an open letter by the Irish Sport for Palestine Group, signed by over 160 Irish sportspeople, urging the Football Association of Ireland (FAI) to withdraw from the fixtures because of the situation in Gaza.

O'Shea said it is important for the squad to "speak openly" and "respect each other's views" when they come together to discuss the Israel game on Friday.

"We've got to respect each other's opinions and each other's views and really sit down and take the time, because it deserves the time to talk about," he said.

"It's the main thing and it's something that can't be brushed over. Whatever decision that we go through as players is taken as one and everybody's view is respected as well.

O'Shea, who will captain the Republic of Ireland in the absence of the injured Nathan Collins, added the players have been aware of the "noise" surrounding this window but have tried to avoid it as much as possible.

"The good thing we have as players is when we step into the squad you're in the international bubble straight away," added the Ipswich defender.

"So we've known the noise around the game and there has been, but I think we've all tried to stay off social media as much as possible and stay together."

Israel FA comments on Hallgrimsson 'unacceptable' - Martin

Neutral venues and no 'away' fans - how Israel v Republic of Ireland became so contentious

Uefa rejected request to keep Republic of Ireland and Israel separate - FAI

O'Shea admitted it was a "difficult" and "unusual" situation for the players, who will also face Israel in the Republic of Ireland's 'home' game in the Serbian town of Backa Topola on 4 October.

"We've got a massive game tomorrow that we've been preparing for," he said.

"We've come in on Sunday and that's been our focus straight away was preparing for that game and giving it the amount of effort that it needs.

"Kosovo are a great side and we've been preparing for that."

In February 2024, the Ireland women's basketball team refused to shake hands with Israel and lined up for their anthem beside the team's bench rather than the centre of the court.

Asked if a decision had been made about pre-match formalities, O'Shea said: "We spoke already at the start of the week that we're going to come together on Friday and discuss this as a group.

"Tomorrow we've got a game to focus on, first of all. I don't think we'll be doing our job properly if we didn't put our full focus into that game. Once the game's over and Friday comes, we're all going to come together as one and discuss it openly."

When asked if a boycott of Sunday's Israel game will be discussed among the squad on Friday, O'Shea said: "For us, the decision was made by the FAI, Uefa and the Government. For us as players, that's not our decision.

"We're Irish players and when called upon we come and represent our country and that's important to know too.

"Obviously when we come together, we'll speak openly about what we feel and what we feel is right. And yeah, that'll be given its time on Friday."

Earlier this week, Israel's football governing body accused Republic of Ireland head coach Heimir Hallgrimmson of "ignorance, hypocrisy and stupidity" regarding comments he made about facing Israel.

Last week, Hallgrimsson said: "We're not playing with genocide, we're playing against genocide. We're playing against Israel, we're not playing with Israel."

While the FAI did not respond publicly, Taoiseach Micheal Martin [Irish prime minister] said Israel FA's comments were "unacceptable" and "should be withdrawn".

Addressing the matter on Wednesday, Hallgrimsson expressed gratitude for the support he has received while admitting "it was not clever" of him to generate headlines in the build-up to the Kosovo match.

"Obviously, we are grateful for all the support that we have," said the Icelander, who has been in charge since 2024.

"Creating and taking over maybe the headlines at the moment, what I said [in the] last press meeting we had is taking the attention away from maybe what's most important," he said.

"We are playing an important game against Kosovo. So that was not the purpose and from a leadership point of view, it was not clever from me to take the attention like this.

"I need to be focused on the game, the players need to be focused on the game. But to answer the question, we're thankful for all the support we get. It's a tricky time for us."

Armed Palestinian group Hamas attacked Israel on 7 October 2023, killing about 1,200 people and taking 251 hostages.

In response, Israel launched a massive military offensive in Gaza, during which more than 73,000 people have been killed, according to the territory's Hamas-run health ministry, whose figures are considered reliable by the United Nations.

Israel has repeatedly denied that it has committed genocide, as well as war crimes and crimes against humanity. It says its military operations in Gaza have been conducted in self-defence and in accordance with international law.

title: Antonelli on 'stepping up' after 2024 crash 'stayed in my head for a very long time'
description: Championship leader Kimi Antonelli tells BBC Sport how he is "still finding my way" in F1 after a 2024 crash "stayed in my head for a very long time".
fullText:
Kimi Antonelli says he knew from the first moment he drove this year's Mercedes that he would be transformed as a Formula 1 driver in 2026.

The 20-year-old Italian, who is running away with the world championship in only his second season in F1, is reflecting on his breakthrough year in the sport in an exclusive interview with BBC Sport.

A difficult debut season last year had left external expectations of Antonelli low at the start of 2026. But on a typically damp and cold January day at Silverstone, he already sensed that something special might be on the cards.

"It was just a few laps in the wet," Antonelli says, "but I just felt better in the car, much better than I felt last year. Also the car felt well, but I just felt better mentally in the car. Less tense, more relaxed and more mature."

Last year, he says, was "not great". "I was driving very tense most of the time, I wasn't able to extract the potential out of me," he says.

"This year, it's a lot different. The mindset has been the biggest change."

Fast forward eight months and the effects of that new headspace are plain to see.

After 14 grands prix, and with either eight or nine remaining depending on the war in the Middle East, Antonelli is a massive 81 points clear of team-mate George Russell.

Not only that, but he looks so in control. Always fast, always composed, a factor in every grand prix. Everyone knows the championship is basically over, barring some kind of dramatic misfortune.

Even then, Antonelli says he is "still finding my way" in F1.

The journey Antonelli has been on in the past two years is remarkable, and he says even he is "surprised" by the extent of his progress this year.

He was comprehensively outperformed by Russell in 2025. So when it was obvious that Mercedes would start the new regulatory era with an advantage, it was the Briton who started the season as championship favourite.

Russell duly won the opening race in Australia, but Antonelli was less than three seconds behind him at the flag. This, he says, was the second moment of realisation of what might be possible.

"I had a big, big crash in FP3," Antonelli recalls. "But then thanks to the mechanics - who all throughout the season have done an incredible job, but on that specific occasion, it is a miracle - I was able to go back in the car and push again in the high speed and getting close to the limit.

"The crash, definitely it compromised a little bit qualifying and the race because we couldn't set up properly the car. I mean, the car was still very quick. But it was not easy.

"Still being able to stay close despite that, I was like, 'OK, you know, it's not going to be a walk in the park. It's going to be very tough', but I knew already that it was a different story compared to last year.

"If it would have happened last year, I wouldn't have been able to overcome that."

Antonelli's first season in F1 was haunted by an incident that happened the first time he drove on a grand prix weekend.

At the 2024 Italian Grand Prix, the day before they formally announced Antonelli was the replacement for Ferrari-bound Lewis Hamilton, Mercedes gave him an outing in first practice at Monza.

He was blindingly fast on his first flying lap - but then crashed heavily on his second.

Team principal Toto Wolff played it down at the time, saying he was well aware there would be mistakes from Antonelli as he found his feet in F1. But behind the scenes the incident had had a big impact on the young man.

"Monza stayed in my head for a very long time," Antonelli says. "I think all throughout last season, at least. Definitely that was a big thing that was kind of slowing me down.

"This memory of being afraid to do a mistake, also because going through the difficult period (in the middle of 2025), this memory was even stronger in my head, if you know what I mean.

"Because it was already a difficult period and I was like, 'If I even do a mistake or I crash, it's even worse.'

"So yeah, it's been a thing that has been bothering me a lot last year. This year I was able to just put it behind."

Doing so has involved a lot of work behind the scenes, analysing what happened in 2025, understanding what had gone well, what had not, and why, and what he could do to improve.

"The mindset going into this season, it was mainly trying to be able to extract more out of my potential," Antonelli says. "Trying to, first of all, do a better job than previous year. But as well trying to put things more together.

"The preparation that I did in pre-season was very, very intense. But it helped me a lot to arrive ready for this season.

"Plus, I did a lot of work with my mental coach. Trying to get my head right, my thoughts right on understanding the goal, and understanding that the most important thing is to be ready and to stay present in the moment.

"Not trying to think about final results or what would happen if I wouldn't achieve that. But just trying to be present and trying to do the best with what you can do in the moment."

Still, though, he admits to be "definitely surprised" at how much progress he has made.

"I knew that I was going to be better than my first year," he says. "Obviously, because I think last year, towards the end of the season, I started to put things more together, starting to extract more performance. But still, it was still not great.

"Whereas this year, it's a lot different. Also as well, with the first win, the first pole, it took a lot of weight off my shoulder."

Antonelli has blossomed. Everything seems to be coming so easily to him. If he drops back in a race, he recovers seamlessly and quickly. Overtaking moves are done quickly and decisively. There's not been a circuit on which he has lacked pace.

Russell, by contrast, has admitted to struggling and - while not trying to take anything away from Antonelli, who he is always quick to praise - has expressed his opinion that his his driving style does not suit this year's new cars.

All of which raises a key question - how much of what is happening this year is Antonelli stepping it up, and how much Russell falling back?

"That's a very difficult question," Antonelli says. "I've definitely stepped up.

"This year definitely everything is new. So it requires also a little bit of a different approach. And trying to adapt to a different car, which hasn't been easy."

His consistency this year, he says, has come from the fact he has found "a nice rhythm in the season".

"I always try to follow my routines," Antonelli says, "the way I approach the weekend. I try to approach it all the time the same.

"I'm still finding my way, but I've found a way that helps me to be consistent and also helps me to be consistently ready when I go in the car."

There are still moments when he misjudges things, though. He cites the Barcelona-Catalunya Grand Prix, just days after his outstanding win in Monaco, one of the most dominant at that storied track for years.

"Monaco was a very high moment for me in the season, and then I went to Barcelona and I was probably a bit too excited, especially over a single lap," he says.

"So I was overdriving, I was chasing the lap time and the result didn't come in qualifying. I was actually a bit far back and didn't do a good lap.

"But that's because I was trying to do a bit too much after a very high moment in my career. And then I understood that that is not the way."

The lesson was applied after his spellbinding win from 19th on the grid at Monza, his home race, a result that Wolff said "closed a cycle" from his 2024 crash.

Antonelli says: "After Monza, I reminded myself, 'Don't make the same mistake as you did after Monaco.'"

He won the Spanish Grand Prix seven days later, an eighth victory from 14 races so far this season.

Success has inevitably led to fame, and with it attention.

"Life has changed a lot," Antonelli says. "I'm not going to lie. It's been a big change, but it's nice to see so much support. Definitely, one side is very nice, but on the other side, you have to be careful. You've got to protect yourself a bit more because obviously you're more exposed."

All year, Antonelli has talked about focusing on process, about doing the best he can on every single day, not thinking about the big picture.

Now, though, for the first time, he acknowledges the title - an achievement that would make him the youngest world champion in F1 history - is on his mind.

"Yes, I thought about it," he says. "But again, thinking about it, I came always to the same conclusion that the earlier I finish all this, the better it is.

"So I've got to just keep pushing. I keep doing the best I can every race. Because, yeah, that's the way. Just not finish. And until it's done, it's not over."

title: England players carrying World Cup scar - Saka
description: England winger Bukayo Saka says the team are still carrying the "scar" of their heartbreaking World Cup semi-final exit to Argentina.
fullText:
England winger Bukayo Saka says the team are still carrying the "scar" of their heartbreaking World Cup semi-final exit to Argentina.

Thomas Tuchel's team were on the verge of becoming the first England side to reach a men's World Cup final since 1966, but were stunned by two late Argentina goals as they fell to a 2-1 loss.

A thrilling 6-4 victory over France in the bronze medal match gave the Three Lions their best World Cup finish in six decades, but the wait for their second trophy goes on.

"Obviously, there is still a scar on us when you believed and everyone was so united and so confident we could do it," Saka said.

"Not just us, but the whole country we felt.

"You try to move on as soon as possible, but you know a scar is a scar, it decides to heal when it heals itself."

England get an immediate reminder of what might have been as they host world champions Spain at Wembley on Saturday (19:45 BST) in the first of four Nations League matches over the next two weeks.

"We are trying to draw a line under [the World Cup] now and focus on the new international season that we have coming up," Saka added.

"We have got four massive, difficult group games to try and qualify us for the Nations League [knockouts] that we are really focused on."

Meanwhile, Saka believes it is only a matter of time before his Arsenal team-mate Max Dowman, 16, earns a senior England call-up.

"I think so," Saka said. "His talent is insane. It's up to him how far he is going to go in football. His talent is crazy."

England Under-21 manager Lee Carsley concurred with Saka on Dowman's "amazing talent" but thinks the youngster staying with the under-19s during this international window is the best option.

"He is more than capable of playing in the under-21s," Carsley said.

"What I do think will happen with the age group he goes to is that he can play the minutes.

title: Man Utd still £1bn in debt with £63.5m spent on new stadium
description: Manchester United's overall debt remains over £1bn despite Sir Jim Ratcliffe's extensive cost-cutting measures, with the club also confirming it has spent £63.5m buying land for their new stadium.
fullText:
Manchester United's overall debt remains over £1bn despite Sir Jim Ratcliffe's extensive cost-cutting measures, with the club also confirming it has spent £63.5m buying land for their new stadium.

Amid a backdrop of fan protests and a disappointing start to the season that has left United 12th in the Premier League and already out of the EFL Cup, United have announced record revenues of £677.6m and a £22.6m operating profit despite not playing in Europe for the first time in a decade.

This represents a huge shift from the £113.2m loss in 2023-24.

However, while they have saved £8.5m of a projected £16.5m pay-off to axed boss Ruben Amorim after he accepted a job at AC Milan, other costs have increased.

Net finance costs for the year were £69.6m, an increase of 228.3%. United put most of this down to a foreign exchange loss. According to football finance expert Kieran Maguire, this sum alone has now exceeded £1bn since the leveraged Glazer family buyout in 2005.

In addition, United also confirmed they spent £63.5m of an additional $125 (£94.14m) added to their historic debt during a summer refinancing move on land for their new stadium. The club has not explained what it has done with the remainder. The stadium itself is likely to cost in excess of £2bn.

It means the club's overall debt, while reducing from £1.3bn at the end of December, is still over £1bn, made up of the historic debt, which now stands at £577.6m, the £111.4m outstanding on its revolving credit facility, and outstanding transfer fees, which club sources say represents approximated 75% of the £473m listed and being owed as 'trade and other payables'.

This comes at a time when supporters are furious about what they believe to be chronic under investment in Michael Carrick's first team squad this summer.

United spent £148m on three new signings - Carlos Baleba, Andrey Santos and Youri Tielemans - this summer. It was less than a third of the £458m Manchester City invested in their squad and lower even than newly promoted Ipswich.

However, fans are angry there was no additional left-back purchased to provide competition for Luke Shaw, who has missed three matches due to injury already, or striking support for Benjamin Sesko, who missed pre-season as he recovered from a shin complaint that has already resurfaced.

While United argue the additional funds were earmarked for their stadium, to be built 350 yards away from where Old Trafford stands, the loan itself is lodged within club accounts.

"We are pleased to have secured record revenues," said chief executive Omar Berrada.

"This demonstrates the underlying strength of our business, and shows the direct impact of the work we have been doing over the past two years.

"While these results confirm that we are on the right trajectory, we will continue to take a disciplined approach to ensure our finances remain sustainable.

"With that financial sustainability in mind, we have strengthened both our men's and women's teams during the summer window and our men's team has seen the return of Champions League football to Old Trafford."

United have also been criticised for a lack of investment in the Women's Super League squad, which is currently second bottom of the table with one point from three games.

Ratcliffe previously argued the club had to take strong action to slash losses. Two lots of redundancies led to 450 people losing their jobs, while United have confirmed their latest set of salary costs have reduced by £11.3m to £302m.

"This is primarily due to changes in the make-up of the men's first team squad, combined with savings associated with headcount reduction programs implemented over the previous two fiscal years," said the club.

title: Ad break in Women's Champions League was unscheduled
description: Coverage of Arsenal's Women's Champions League opener also featured a dog on set, a vegetable platter and a rotating floor.
fullText:
A three-minute advert break during a Women's Champions League game was not scheduled, Disney+ confirmed.

Arsenal and HB Koge were drawing 0-0 in the second half on Tuesday when coverage was interrupted.

It was one of several technical issues during the coverage, which fans said was "gimmicky" and "undermines" women's football. One guest was a dog with 137,000 Instagram followers.

Disney confirmed it was an unintended interruption caused by a technical issue and understood the frustration caused. It was making steps to ensure it did not happen again.

Arsenal won 1-0 in their first game of this season's competition thanks to a stoppage-time Mariona Caldentey penalty.

Disney's coverage also featured a vegetable platter being served and a rotating floor.

Alex Scott hosted the first show of the season, alongside former England forward Lianne Sanderson, content creators Alex Bailess and Tyra Mills, and a dog called Barley Boy.

There was no explanation for his presence on set other than his Instagram following.

It was the second season of the Women's Champions League to be broadcast on Disney+. Matches are produced by ESPN.

New this season is "The Hangout", described by Disney as a live studio show billed as a "new match-day experience for fans, delivering pre-match build-up, half-time analysis and post-match reaction".

In a media release before the first round of fixtures, Disney said: "The Hangout will combine expert analysis with fresh perspectives and fan engagement."

However, the evening was marred by a series of technical issues – from players waiting to be interviewed but unable to hear questions from the studio, to a rotating floor that appeared to have a mind of its own.

There were also camera shots with cushions blocking the view of Scott, and audio synchronisation problems.

Italian reporter Roberto Perrone, in Milan for Inter Milan's match against Swedish side Hacken, also encountered audio problems.

When the sound returned, viewers were shown a non-football-themed quiz, with questions ranging from types of pasta to Italy's biggest city.

One fan wrote on X: "I think a lot of the problem with the debates in women's football broadcasting over analysis and punditry vs content creation and gimmicky fun, is that in men's football you can get both - and in different shows.

"In women's football, you get one show, and so they try to do it all."

Another fan wrote: "We want women's football to be taken seriously, yet coverage like this undermines that. Personality and fun have their place, but not at the expense of the football.

"The game doesn't need gimmicks to make it interesting. Give the players, the competition and the football itself the same focus, analysis and respect we expect elsewhere in the sport.

"Women's football is more than capable of being the main event."

Megan Feringa, a journalist for the Athletic, said: "Watching Disney's coverage is like going in and out of a lucid dream.

"Why is there a dog? Why is the couch spinning? Why do the adverts cut right into analysis?"

Flo Lloyd-Hughes, a broadcaster and writer for the Cutback, said: "Why does women's football coverage always have to be so gimmicky? It's the Champions League, not Blue Peter.

"Put some pundits who know about the teams in a studio, make sure the tech works and have a decent bit of time for build-up and analysis to contextualise everything."

Last November concerns were raised over the professionalism and legitimacy of the Women's League Cup quarter-final and semi-final draw, which was conducted by social media influencer GK Barry.

In the same month Sky Sports scrapped its new female-focused TikTok channel, Halo, after it faced a backlash online, with its posts described as "patronising" and "sexist".

Disney+ coverage continues on Wednesday with Chelsea hosting Austria Wien at 20:00 BST.

title: Data structure that lets different parts of math work together
description: Composite Machine: Automatic Calculus via Dimensional Arithmetic... and a bit more. - tmilovan/composite-machine
fullText:
After months of experimenting, learning (finding about Levi Civita fields etc.), building and testing different implementations, here is the new release that contains the accumulated findings. This release contains results of trying out different approaches and results of numeruos experiments. The more experimental stuff still relies to external support, oracles etc. (as it should), the more tested features are tending to become more and more self reliant with additional iterations (eg, derivations and integrals.).

Note of caution: this is still highly experimental and most likely (for sure) still contains some misconceptions and a lot of edge cases and other bugs. The purpose of the library is to showcase what is possible and to serve as a baseline for further exploration.

The first proper pypy library based on this experimental features has been released. A standalone tool to evaluate Python functions at points where they're undefined and get exact limit values if they exists.

Automatic calculus via dimensional arithmetic... and a bit more.

A data structure that implements a number system, letting different parts of non-standard (and standard) math work together.

For example, it gives you derivatives, integrals, and limits as a side effect of normal computation. No symbolic engine, no computation graph, no tape. Tag a number, do your math, read the results off the dimensional coefficients.

The residue is infinitesimal, structured, and it contains the derivative of every operation that produced it.

Alpha stage. Research code. The math works, performance doesn't (yet). AGPL-licensed. A PyTorch/CUDA backend is available under commercial license."

Numbers are sparse dicts mapping dimensions to coefficients. A dimension is an integer, or a vector over an iterated-logarithm basis when log-scale terms are in play. Dimension 0 is the value. Negative dimensions store derivative info. Multiply dimensions - turns out that's the same thing as the product rule and chain rule, just expressed as data structure operations.

One evaluation. All derivatives fall out. No separate differentiation pass.

The derivative computation part builds on well-known work: Clifford's dual numbers (1873), Wengert's forward-mode AD (1964), Rall's Taylor arithmetic (1981), Griewank's framework (2000).

The number system has a separate and older lineage. A sparse map from exponents to coefficients, with non-integer exponents and finitely many terms below any given one, is the shape of the Levi-Civita field (Levi-Civita, 1892–1898) - the smallest non-Archimedean ordered field extension of the reals that is real-closed and Cauchy-complete. Letting an exponent be a vector ordered lexicographically instead of a single number gives Hahn series (Hahn, 1907), which is what the iterated-logarithm basis here amounts to: dimensions valued in an ordered group, compared componentwise. The scale those vectors index - x, log x, log log x, ranked by eventual dominance - is du Bois-Reymond's Infinitärcalcül as set out in Hardy's Orders of Infinity (1910), and the Hardy fields built on it. Expansions that mix powers, exponentials and iterated logs are transseries (Écalle, 1992; van der Hoeven, 2006). The infinitesimals themselves are made rigorous by Robinson's non-standard analysis (1966), and the surreals (Conway, 1976) contain the Levi-Civita field as a subfield.

Computing in such a field, rather than reasoning about it, also has prior art. Berz framed automatic differentiation as non-Archimedean analysis (1992), and Shamseddine and Berz developed numerical analysis directly on the Levi-Civita field, including derivatives of functions where classical AD breaks down. Sergeyev's grossone (2003 onward) is the closest in representation: a positional numeral system in powers of an infinite unit ①, with the infinitesimal ①⁻¹, used on an "Infinity Computer" for exact higher-order differentiation, ODE solvers and lexicographic optimization - the same records as the dimensions here, written in a different notation. Grossone keeps the ordinary zero (0·① = 0, ① − ① = 0); this library does not, and that is where the two part ways. The overlap is worth stating plainly: the algebra here is not new, and where this library's structures coincide with those, the credit is theirs.

What this library explores is a different algebraic context for that mechanism. Higher-order terms are preserved instead of truncated. Subtraction retains provenance instead of collapsing to zero. Multiplication by zero shifts structure instead of destroying it. The idea is that if you stop throwing away information at each step, calculus operations become extractable from the algebra.

Does this generalize to everything? Open question. The test suite covers a wide range of standard problems and the results match. Finding the boundaries is the point of this project.

For the theoretical framing, see the paper.

Breadth in one structure, at a cost that depends entirely on the shape of the problem.
The numbers under Performance are measured, not asserted, and they do
not all point the same way.

No L'Hôpital. Plug in the infinitesimal, read the standard part.

ZERO isn't Python's 0 - it's a structural infinitesimal, coefficient 1 at dimension −1. Operations on it are well-defined and reversible:

Not yet implemented or highly experimental:

No single ratio - it depends on what you ask for. Measured on CPython/macOS, float64, one thread,
NumPy 1.26.4, SymPy 1.14.0.

Derivatives. Tag a number, evaluate 1/(1+x) once, read all ten derivatives off the result:

Faster and exact. One evaluation carries every order, while a stencil needs a fresh step size per
order and has run out of digits by order 10.

A single first derivative goes the other way: NumPy does it in 0.2 µs against 35 µs here,
roughly 140x. The crossover is around the third derivative.

Batches. NumPy vectorises and this does not - four orders of magnitude per point. Pythorch and CUDA backends not present here support batching.

Sparse grids. An explicit PDE whose active front stays at 121 cells: 24x faster than a
dense NumPy grid at 200,000 cells, 260x at 2,000,000. Composite time is flat; the dense grid
pays for the whole domain whether anything is happening in it or not.

vs SymPy. Indeterminate limits: 3–70x faster, both exact. A Taylor expansion to order 8:
0.6 ms against 3.7 s, about 6000x, agreeing to 15 digits.

Backend selection. use_dense_series() for calculus - anything with transcendentals builds a
dense, contiguous series, and it is ~1.6x faster there than the alternatives. use_dict() for
pure-arithmetic jets, where there is no series to lay out (~2x faster on 1/(1+x)). The default
use_sparse_dense() is the grid backend: several times slower on either kind of jet, and the one
to keep for sparse supports over a large domain.

A high-performance backend using PyTorch with CUDA and MPS acceleration is available under commercial license. Contact tmilovan@fwd.hr.

Python 3.7+. NumPy is optional (used for FFT-accelerated multiplication).

Or run a single suite directly:

PYTHONPATH=. matters: running a test as a bare script puts tests/ on the
import path rather than the repo root, so composite resolves to whatever is
installed instead of the working copy.

839 tests across thirteen suites, all passing.
