title: Hunting hidden gems - is there anywhere in the world left to scout?
description: Through live scouting and increasing data and footage, top clubs now have tabs on a large proportion of the world's talent.
fullText:
The world's biggest clubs were all aware of the teenage sensation turning heads for Universidad de Chile, the one dubbed his generation's Alexis Sanchez.

"When we signed Dario Osorio, it was not because no-one knew about him," Kristian Kjaer, technical director at Midtjylland, tells BBC Sport.

Osorio was on the radar of AC Milan, RB Leipzig, Salzburg and a number of other English and German clubs before he left Santiago for Denmark at the age of 19.

It was a carefully considered pathway. After three seasons in Scandinavia, the winger joined Crystal Palace on loan this summer with a £24m option to buy which would make him the most expensive sale in Danish Superliga history.

Midtjylland, where Brentford owner Matthew Benham was a majority stakeholder between 2014 and 2023, are renowned as one of the most innovative clubs in Europe for their use of analytics - from set-pieces to smart recruitment.

"We work on both pathways," explains Kjaer. "We have subjective scouting, more classic video scouting, live scouting, a network, people we trust in the club and also our partners. And then we have the data scouting.

"And Dario Osorio, we were aware of him long before we signed him."

From feet-on-the-ground to the increasing availability of footage, data analytics and artificial intelligence, Premier League clubs - whether buying direct from source or tracking players like Osorio's progress - have a large proportion of the world's emerging talent covered.

"That hidden gem kind of thing almost does not exist any 

"You would put this period as one of the most transformational in talent ID and recruitment," explains Sam Turner, head of operations at scouting and development platform Eyeball.

Clubs can now obtain an incredible level of detail on players across the globe before they have even made a senior appearance. Eyeball, for example, was founded five years ago to focus on those predominantly aged 13 to 21.

It is used by more than 60% of clubs in Europe's top five leagues, and a majority of Premier League sides, for access to more than 400,000 young players across 42 global markets from Europe to Africa and Latin America.

Winger Malick Yalcouye, a new 20-year-old star at Brighton, was tracked on the system since developing at Ivorian side ASEC Mimosas, likewise Bazoumana Toure, who is now at Newcastle.

The breadth of coverage is highlighted by other recent moves - Josue Caicedo left Ecuador's LDU Quito for Barcelona, Mustapha Nyassi swapped Gambia's Real de Banjul for Copenhagen and Nour Ashraf joined Leipzig from Egypt's ENPPI.

"The availability of data and footage has prompted a change in methodology," says Turner. "That has brought a load of benefits in terms of data-led recruitment, time saving, cost saving."

Eyeball takes north of 2,000 data points every match, typically from leading amateur clubs and elite academies who film and upload their fixtures.

The result is a huge database allowing analysts to watch all of a player's progressive passes, for example, discover who covered the most distance or simply ask 'find me a player like Ashley Cole'.

"There is always this human feel that can never be lost," adds Turner. "I like to think we have aided scouts and recruitment teams, supplemented them with the tools, data, information to be able to make more informed decisions on a more consistent basis."

Data, says Midtjylland's Kjaer, is "extremely important because it gives you an objective tool you can lean towards" when complemented by years of decision-making experience.

"We cannot just turn on the computer and it tell us who to sign and then we go sign them," he says. "We also need to know about the cultural background, the family background, to make sure they fit into our football club.

"Of course, data has given us opportunities. We sign young. So the sample size will simply be smaller for us because if we are waiting until it's big enough, Brighton and Liverpool and Brentford and other guys, they will sign the player in front of us."

"We can find interesting players all around the world," explains Kjaer.

"I like us to be open-minded. We are particular in the way we play and the way we sell. And therefore, we need to find these players who fit that style of play.

"When you have done your due diligence and you feel certain, pull the trigger. The pace in decision-making is also a hidden gem."

One country regularly mentioned is Uzbekistan, who played in their first World Cup this summer, while Turner says Azerbaijan is pioneering a national talent network and "very forward-thinking and motivated to progress the game domestically".

Then there is Japan, which Turner calls a "guiding star" in youth development for a system which takes players from grassroots, to school and college football and then the professional game. Think Kaoru Mitoma's thesis on dribbling techniques.

For European clubs, it makes identifying young Japanese prospects more complex.

Latin America, too, remains a hotbed of talent.

As former Midtjylland chairman Rasmus Ankersen, who has since worked for Brentford and Southampton, wrote in his book The Gold Mine Effect, a club such as Cruzeiro will reject 4,000 players under the age of 15 for every one they take in.

Brazilian clubs are naturally protective of their assets.

"They know eventually players will leave," says Turner. "But it is allowing them to leave at the right age where those clubs can benefit locally. And we are very invested in that."

Much of the region, however, remains "untapped" but recording games creates opportunities.

"It's just a visibility piece for a lot of these players that means they don't get picked up," says Turner.

"We have gone a long way in solving that for a lot of markets, but there are many more that can be picked up with brilliant players everywhere."

One of those markets continues to be Africa.

"There'll be thousands," says Thomas Randolph, founder of Delphlyx, when asked whether talented African players may have missed out on big moves in the past.

Delphlyx works with Premier League clubs and ownership groups, and others across Europe, the United States and Mexico, to provide information on the best - and most relevant - 14 to 21-year-olds in West Africa, often through data, live scouting and private tournaments.

"We have over 19,000 players in Africa on our platform that you could just sit right here in London and watch, then pick up the phone, call one of them and organise a trial or a transfer. That just wasn't happening before," adds Randolph.

With a projected average age of just over 18, Randolph says the region is a "young, growing, developing space" - a "sporting mecca". Football remains the main passion, though NFL and NBA are starting to invest in certain countries.

But Randolph disputes the idea African scouting is now saturated, citing a number of areas that remain relatively undiscovered, often because of conflict or logistics, with scouts drawn to the region's biggest cities.

"Zadok Yohanna is a good example," explains Randolph. "He moved to Brighton recently. He comes from Ikon Allah, which is a tiny and relatively unknown academy in northern Nigeria.

"The southern bit of Senegal is where Sadio Mane is from, where [Lamine] Camara is from, who Chelsea tried to sign, and there's only one team down there. So within all these big countries, there are certain regions that are less scouted."

Historically, it was agents who brought players out of Africa rather than scouts discovering them, whereas Delphlyx aims to help clubs identify and analyse certain talent first so scouts can visit specific tournaments or showcases to watch targets.

Randolph mentions eastern Mali, Togo, Guinea-Bissau and Burkina Faso but Benin, situated between Nigeria and Togo, is of particular interest for the way the country has invested federation grants in football infrastructure and pitches.

"One place they've used the Fifa money very well is Benin," says Randolph. "It's now produced probably a future female Ballon d'Or winner - Romaine Gandonou, who's 15, just played at the Under-20 World Cup, and got the likes of PSG, Barcelona, everyone after her.

"Benin is going to be a country that over the next few years will become very interesting."

Some Premier League clubs are buying directly from Africa. At 18, Senegalese defender Mor Talla Ndiaye has already been on the bench for Liverpool after arriving from Amitie, owned by ex-Newcastle and Chelsea striker Demba Ba.

Ndiaye was spotted at last year's Under-17 World Cup, where Burkina Faso midfielder Mohamed Zongo also impressed. He will join Chelsea and Strasbourg owners BlueCo's project when he turns 18 in two years' time.

"The Under-17 World Cup is a big one," says Randolph. "If your African nation plays there and you do well, you're going to get a good move."

Scouts have also been at the recent Under-17 Africa Cup of Nations qualifying and Delphlyx has helped organise trials for players from Senegal and Gambia at Premier League clubs.

The pool is narrowed, however, because players must obtain a Governing Body Endorsement to be granted a work permit or - most likely - take one of a club's four Elite Significant Contribution spots, which essentially comes down to how many youth or senior internationals they have played.

It's part of the reason young players initially move to European countries where regulations are less stringent and why Randolph believes Scottish clubs, where the same criteria does not apply, should be looking into the African market the way Scandinavians do.

Nordsjaelland are unique in that the Right to Dream academy - founded in Ghana in 1999 by former Manchester United scout Tom Vernon - bought the Danish club seven years ago to provide a pathway for its biggest prospects, which have included Mohammed Kudus, Simon Adingra and Kamaldeen Sulemana.

Brighton's Yalcouye and Newcastle's Toure made their first moves to Swedish clubs IFK Goteborg and Hammarby, while Midtjylland have a partner club in Nigeria, FC Ebedei. Coventry's Frank Onyeka played for both on his way to the Premier League, as did Paul Onuachu, now at Trabzonspor.

Like with Osorio, and others such as Guinea-Bissau forward Franculino, who left this summer for Trabzonspor, or Ivory Coast defender Ousmane Diomande, now at Nottingham Forest via Sporting, Midtjylland can highlight a track record of developing young players before selling them on.

"I see Midtjylland a bit like Silicon Valley for tech companies - we have produced so much talent over the years," explains Kjaer.

"We can focus only on the development. Of course, we need to win, but it's a bit more of a secure environment.

"What we say is, if you want to focus on your career as a football player, you have to come here because that is the only thing we do. That is what we are experts in."

There remains, however, undiscovered talent close to home. France, particularly Paris, boasts an incredibly rich talent pool.

A unique national youth league system, where amateur sides face professional academies - and regularly beat them - offers clubs the chance to witness unsigned prospects competing against the most gifted players in their age group.

"Scouts from all over the world come to Ile-de-France to look at players in our leagues," said Jamel Sandjak, president of the Ligue de Paris Ile-de-France, which boasts more than 1,000 clubs and 270,000 players.

"Most of the France national youth teams are full of our players. So our regional teams are playing at national level."

Last season, amateur side ES Nanterre, from the outskirts of Paris, won Championnat National Group B ahead of Champions League outfits Lens and Lille and second-tier clubs Reims, Bastia and Red Star.

Forward Exauce Luyindula was the division's top scorer for renowned amateurs AAS Sarcelles - where Riyad Mahrez played until he was 18 - and has since joined Ligue 2 Guingamp.

Other Eyeball, external partners enjoyed memorable victories, too. AFC Creil beat Lens at under-15 level, Olympique Rovenain's under-19s beat Nice and CS Bretigny's under-17s edged Paris St-Germain.

"Until recently, the vast majority of clubs were relying on the fact the best players are in the best academies or national talent systems, when actually a lot of those players were chosen by 12 or 13," explains Turner.

"A lot of the time that can be right, but also statistically the best players at 12 aren't always the best players at 18.

"There is such a high concentration of players in that region, there is not enough space. The best players aren't necessarily in the national systems."

title: 'Be comfortable in your own identity' - Agassi's advice to Raducanu
description: As Emma Raducanu plots a route back to the pinnacle of tennis, the Briton is taking inspiration from Andre Agassi's 2009 autobiography.
fullText:
As Emma Raducanu plots a route back to the pinnacle of tennis, the Briton has been taking inspiration from Andre Agassi's 2009 autobiography.

Five years have passed since Raducanu's remarkable US Open triumph, when at the age of 18 she became the first qualifier in the Open era to win a Grand Slam.

American Agassi was a teenage prodigy himself and later claimed the first of his eight major singles titles at Wimbledon in 1992 aged 22.

But between the peak years of his career, he had to overcome a challenging period when he went four years without a major and dropped to 141st in the world rankings.

"I was especially intrigued by the passage where he got out of his slump in the late 1990s by creating his own training regimen and finding his way back to the top," Raducanu told Uniqlo.

"It speaks in depth about his early successes and the lows he reached, perhaps as a result of them.

"A lot of it was so relatable."

Agassi said his hope was for his experiences to help other players going through similar periods in their own careers.

"It's wonderful to hear that anybody can relate," Agassi told BBC Breakfast.

"It was literally the hope that if one person read it and it gave them hope, some tools to understand that they're not alone, they can figure it out and get to a healthier place without having to direct their frustrations at the game of tennis, then it was a success for me.

"So, hearing that 17 years later it can still impact somebody, especially in this game, it does make me feel good."

Raducanu reached a career-high ranking of 10 in July 2022, but the 23-year-old has slipped to 98th in the world.

Her progress continues to be hampered by physical issues, and she most recently missed the US Open as she continues her recovery from a stress fracture in her lower right leg.

A foot injury disrupted her pre-season training before she spent two-and-a-half months off court with a post-viral illness earlier this year.

But Raducanu enjoyed one of the best weeks of her career at Queen's Club in June, reaching her biggest final since her triumph in New York five years ago.

Agassi won all four of the sport's Grand Slams and claimed Olympic singles gold at the 1996 Games.

Asked what advice he would give Raducanu, Agassi said: "I would encourage her to focus on being the best of herself on a daily basis, but don't judge that by results or thinking that somehow you have to be 100%.

"You have to learn to be 100% of whatever percent you're at [and] be comfortable in your own identity inside of that - not what people say.

"Back in my day, I could just put down the paper and not read it. Now it seems like it's harder for these youngsters to avoid."

Keothavong 'can't fault' GB after BJK Cup loss to Czechs

GB dominate Ecuador to reach Davis Cup Finals

For Agassi, tennis was by no means a childhood passion. His father, keen for his son to become the very best, would introduce him to others as a future number one tennis player.

That additional pressure, Agassi says, led him to play with "fear". It was not until he sank from world number one to 141st that he felt able to reconnect with the sport.

Agassi, who created a foundation providing education for under-served children during that time, said: "I had more success from that point forward than I did playing out of fear.

"The first thing I would advise a parent to think about is that it's not their life, it's their child.

"You raise a child in their way and they'll never depart from it. You just have to find out what their way is."

Agassi will captain Team USA in the Laver Cup at The O2 in London later this week, between 25-27 September.

"Tennis is a hamster wheel of sorts - the fact that these guys make room in their schedule to play this incredible event tells you how great this event is," Agassi added.

"We're obviously playing Team Europe, in Europe, so I don't know where the crowd is going to have their heart.

"But I know one thing - they're going to see some spectacular tennis."

title: Hadjar to stay as Verstappen's Red Bull team-mate for 2027
description: Frenchman Isack Hadjar is to stay at Red Bull as Max Verstappen's team-mate for the 2027 season.
fullText:
Frenchman Isack Hadjar is to stay at Red Bull as Max Verstappen's team-mate for the 2027 season.

The 21-year-old was promoted to the senior team this season after a rookie year with Racing Bulls and has managed to be closer to Verstappen on pace than any team-mate since Daniel Ricciardo in 2018.

His best result this season came with a third place at the Monaco Grand Prix.

Red Bull team principal Laurent Mekies described the move as "an easy decision".

Mekies said: "Since joining us at the start of the year, Isack has been superb on and off track, especially considering this is only his second F1 season."

Hadjar returns to Red Bull for this weekend's Azerbaijan Grand Prix after missing the past three races with a broken wrist, an injury sustained while boxing as part of his training programme.

Mekies added: "You could see from his first weekend in Melbourne that he handled the step up with remarkable composure and had earned his place in this seat.

"The period since his injury has been a difficult one for Isack, but this extension shows how much we believe in him."

Hadjar said: "I came to this team eight months ago and immediately understood the scale and ambition of this organisation.

"There are so many talented people at the factory, and you're aware of the privilege of driving for such an incredible team alongside a four-time world champion like Max.

"I'm constantly looking to listen, learn and push myself further every single day, which only makes me more excited about what lies ahead."

Over the first half of the season, Hadjar was 0.239 seconds slower than Verstappen on average in qualifying and has managed to out-qualify the Dutchman three times, in Australia, Japan and Britain.

In Silverstone Verstappen had a down-on-power engine and in Australia the Dutchman crashed at the start of qualifying.

Verstappen signed a two-year extension to his contract, that now runs to the end of 2030, in August.

title: New UK agency to fight ‘information warfare’ from likes of Russia, Burnham tells UN
description:
PM aims to ‘stem poisonous tide’ of disinformation and deepfakes with National Centre for Information Defence
Security chiefs will set up a new national centre to tackle disinformation and deepfakes from hostile states such as Russia, Andy Burnham has announced, saying the government had a duty to “stem the poisonous tide” from damaging British interests.
The National Centre for Information Defence will “detect, attribute and disrupt” information attacks by foreign powers, many of which are enabled by AI, bringing together the intelligence agencies, law enforcement and social media companies.
 Continue reading...
fullText:
PM aims to ‘stem poisonous tide’ of disinformation and deepfakes with National Centre for Information Defence

Security chiefs will set up a new national centre to tackle disinformation and deepfakes from hostile states such as Russia, Andy Burnham has announced, saying the government had a duty to “stem the poisonous tide” from damaging British interests.

The National Centre for Information Defence will “detect, attribute and disrupt” information attacks by foreign powers, many of which are enabled by AI, bringing together the intelligence agencies, law enforcement and social media companies.

It will be tasked with making sure the UK has the defensive capability necessary to combat information warfare and build national resilience by helping communities to identify and combat disinformation, preventing a “distorted and untrue” narrative about the UK.

Burnham said the country would have to go into the next decade “eyes wide open” about “insidious” campaigns, many of which had been orchestrated by Russia, which “twisted” what people at home felt about their own country and community.

In eye-catching remarks, the prime minister suggested that Britons who were struggling with the cost of living and young people not in education, training or employment may be particularly susceptible to foreign influence online, underlining how inequality further undermined society.

In his speech to the UN in New York on Tuesday night, Burnham said: “We’re talking about an insidious campaign that reaches into people’s homes and twists what they feel about their own country and community – creating a narrative of decline, stoking division and sowing despair.

“On top of that, we have seen cyber-attacks on our companies and institutions. We know that AI will multiply the threat. We have tiptoed around this for too long. Over the last decade we have given too much ground to those who want to run a negative, corrosive narrative about life in Britain, which bears no resemblance to reality. Well, no more.

“We are going to face the new decade in a different way – with our eyes wide open. We are going to be much prouder in standing up for our values and the rule of law. And we are going to help our people to strengthen their resilience – because, faced with this information warfare, security starts in every home.”

Burnham’s speech came after Donald Trump – during a press conference at the UN with Ukraine’s president Volodymyr Zelenskyy – said that Keir Starmer’s rhetoric had been “too tough” towards Moscow and that London “needs to be a little bit careful”.

Downing Street pushed back on the US president’s remarks, saying that every UK prime minister – up to and including Burnham – had been consistent in the view that Russia’s threats, whether hybrid attacks or rhetoric, were “egregious and unacceptable”.

“The UK is united with our allies on the importance of defending ourselves, and Russia’s aggression will not deter us from supporting Ukraine,” the prime minister’s official spokesperson added.

In his speech, Burnham singled out Russia, saying the Kremlin spent around £1.3bn each year on manipulating information.

“Russian agencies have used every means at their disposal to spread lies and disinformation and prey on people’s fears. They’ve used bots and fake websites. Falsified newspaper articles,” he said.

“Forged the branding of 28 British organisations – including universities and the BBC. They’ve amplified far-right narratives. And we have evidence that they tried to interfere with the 2019 general election.

“We also know that they have tried to stoke tensions and unrest in the wake of horrific events. The idea that anyone would try to use such things to their advantage is just repulsive – but it is what they do.”

The prime minister suggested that certain groups of people who felt their own lives were not improving may be more vulnerable to disinformation and deepfakes.

“If you’re struggling with the cost of living and your life is not improving – or if you’re a young person not in employment, education or training – then you are going to be much more vulnerable to this kind of influence,” he said.

“So part of the challenge is to lift our people up and create the opportunities they need. When inequalities grow too wide, our societies are at greater risk. So we will work to make life more affordable. And we will put in place the architecture we need to stem this poisonous tide.”

The UK plans to share its experience of being on the receiving end of information attack with other countries, and has already supported Moldova, for example, to protect its elections from Russian interference.

“As more elections approach across Europe, more nations are grappling with these issues – some for the first time. So we’re ready to share our understanding of how these actors work, and how we can respond – because this is vital for our collective security and resilience,” Burnham added.

Emily Thornberry, the chair of the foreign affairs select committee, said: “I’m absolutely delighted the prime minister has announced a new centre to tackle the threat of disinformation, which was the major recommendation of the foreign affairs committee’s March 2026 disinformation diplomacy report.

 “For too long, the approach of successive governments to disinformation has been disjointed and without organisation, allowing states like Russia to amplify lies about this country, to sow division and stoke tensions. This new National Centre for Information Defence is an opportunity to finally take on this very serious threat.”

fullText:
A man is recovering from injuries he sustained Sunday morning after ICE officers mistakenly targeted him in a Chicago suburb.

In one video verified by NBC News, a Black man is seen sprawled on the street, near a curb, behind a black SUV in Evanston, Illinois. Two agents wearing ICE-style vests are seen standing over him. One of the agents has his face covered and is wearing a vest that reads “POLICE,” and the other appears to be pinning the man down to the ground. The man is shouting at them and can be heard saying, “I’m a f------ U.S. citizen.”

According to Evanston police, the man reported injuries to his head, neck and teeth, and officers on the scene requested an ambulance.

Police said they are investigating the incident, which was recorded by bystanders and gained attention after being posted on social media.

One bystander in the background of the video is heard saying the ICE officers used force against the man. Other bystanders begin shouting at the man on the ground, asking him if he is OK. The ICE officers eventually get in the black SUV and drive off, leaving the man on the ground. The bystanders begin trying to help the man and call Evanston police.

“I saw two agents pinning down a gentleman. They were using very rough force on him, and it looked like they really did hurt him because we had to call 911,” Miguel Angel Olivares, one of the people who witnessed the encounter, told NBC Chicago on Monday.

“When we saw him, he had his jaw swollen and he had a little blood on his shirt. I’m not sure if it was the agent’s or it was his blood,” Olivares said.

In a news release Sunday, Evanston police said they spoke to an ICE agent who said federal immigration officers “had attempted to identify an individual who resembled a person they were seeking.” After the man refused to provide identification, he was “detained for fingerprinting, and resisted detention.”

An Evanston police officer reported observing blood on the agent’s hands. The agent said he was injured while attempting to handcuff the individual and declined medical treatment, according to the news release from Evanston police. “Agents later determined he was not the person they were seeking and learned that he was a U.S. citizen. He was released.”

A Department of Homeland Security spokesperson told NBC News in a statement Tuesday that their officers encountered a person who resembled someone they were targeting in an enforcement operation in Evanston on Sunday.

“ICE approached the individual and immediately identified themselves as law enforcement. The individual was given lawful commands but was not cooperative and refused to identify himself. ICE officers relied on their training and later left the scene without further incident once the individual finally identified himself,” the DHS statement reads. “DHS enforcement operations are highly targeted, and officers do their due diligence.”

DHS did not state anything about the injuries the man suffered and why ICE officers did not appear to render aid.

Neither the police nor DHS identified the man who was injured.

Evanston police said they spoke with the injured man at a local hospital on Sunday. They “photographed and documented his injuries” as part of an ongoing investigation into the incident, police said.

fullText:
Hundreds of consumers are suing the manufacturers of GLP-1 receptor agonists, alleging the medications may increase the risk of a rare form of vision loss.

The patients behind the lawsuits allege that the medications caused NAION (nonarteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy), according to The Wall Street Journal.

NAION is a rare eye condition in which blood flow to the optic nerve is suddenly reduced, leading to sudden vision loss.

POPULAR GLP-1 WEIGHT-LOSS DRUGS LINKED TO POTENTIALLY DEADLY BRAIN DISORDER

It is the most common cause of acute optic nerve injury in adults over age 50, according to the American Academy of Ophthalmology and the National Eye Institute, which describes it as an "eye stroke."

"The problem with NAION is there's no treatment," Dr. Douglas Lazzaro, an ophthalmologist at NYU Langone Health, told Fox News Digital. "So it can cause some very profound vision loss."

The companies in question, Novo Nordisk (maker of Ozempic and Wegovy) and Eli Lilly (maker of Mounjaro and Zepbound), have disputed the allegations, according to the WSJ report.

POPULAR ERECTILE DYSFUNCTION DRUG LINKED TO EYE DISEASE THAT CAN CAUSE IRREVERSIBLE VISION LOSS

Novo Nordisk called the lawsuits meritless and pointed to company-funded research finding no increased risk of NAION with its drugs. Eli Lilly said it continues to monitor safety data and maintained that current studies do not prove GLP-1 medications cause the condition.

Fox News Digital reached out to the companies requesting comment.

Most of the published research to date has examined semaglutide, rather than tirzepatide.

In a data analysis of 37 million adults published in JAMA Ophthalmology in 2025, researchers found that people using semaglutide experienced a modest increase in NAION risk compared to people taking SGLT2 inhibitors, another class of diabetes medication.

DOCTORS REVEAL HIDDEN DANGER FOR SOME OZEMPIC, WEGOVY USERS WITH BRAIN DISORDERS

A 2024 Harvard Medical School study, published in the same journal, found that patients with type 2 diabetes who were prescribed semaglutide had approximately a fourfold higher relative risk of developing NAION. The absolute risk remained very low.

The authors of both studies noted that the research was observational and could not prove that the medication caused NAION. They emphasized that more evidence is needed.

The FDA has said it is reviewing available evidence regarding a possible association between semaglutide and NAION. The agency has not concluded that semaglutide causes NAION and has not issued a safety warning for semaglutide medications.

The European Medicines Agency concluded there is sufficient evidence of a possible association to recommend adding NAION as a "very rare" adverse reaction to semaglutide product information in Europe.

Lazzaro agreed that "whether or not that's statistically significant is hard to assess, because there were so many variables in this and it's hard to exactly match patients."

"But when they removed all of what they felt were confounding variables … how obese were the patients, male versus female, age, hypertension, level of obesity … they did find that there was a higher risk of NAION."

NAION typically causes sudden, painless vision loss in one eye, per the AAO. Other symptoms may include blurred or dim vision, loss of peripheral vision, or decreased color vision.

Symptoms tend to develop first thing in the morning after waking up.

The biggest risk factors for the condition include age, diabetes, high blood pressure, high cholesterol, obstructive sleep apnea and smoking. As many people taking GLP-1 drugs have diabetes or obesity, some of these underlying risk factors could be factors in vision issues, experts note.

Diabetes itself is a well-established risk factor for NAION, making it difficult for observational studies to separate the effects of the disease from those of the medication, experts have noted.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES

Vision loss from NAION is often permanent. While some patients may regain partial vision over time, there is no proven treatment that can reverse the optic nerve damage.

The condition is rare, with roughly two to 10 cases per 100,000 people each year, depending on the population studied.

Experts emphasize that patients should not stop taking a prescribed GLP-1 medication without first speaking with their healthcare provider. For many people with diabetes or obesity, the medications' proven benefits may outweigh any potential vision risk.

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

When discussing NAION, one important factor is what doctors call a "disc at risk," referring to certain characteristics of the optic disc, or optic nerve.

"So if I had a patient who had what I would see on exam is a disk at risk, a very compact optic nerve where everything's crowded, I would tell that patient probably to not go on a semaglutide," Lazzaro advised.

"My overall take on the matter is there's probably a slightly increased risk of NAION when using the semaglutides, but I think the health benefits outweigh the risks," he went on.

"And unless I have a patient with a disk at risk, I would probably tell them to go on them if they're going to be a lot healthier from an overall standpoint."

title: AOC opens up about her race and gender in weighing a possible White House bid
description:
Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y., raised concerns during an interview published Tuesday about how her race and gender could factor into a potential 2028 presidential bid.
"Pretty candidly, I think about my identity," Ocasio-Cortez said in an interview with The New York Times.
fullText:
Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y., raised concerns during an interview published Tuesday about how her race and gender could factor into a potential 2028 presidential bid.

"Pretty candidly, I think about my identity," Ocasio-Cortez said in an interview with The New York Times. "I’m not naïve to the fact that we are living under a very regressive administration, and I happen to be a woman, and I, you know, happen to be Latina. And I think that there’s a lot of conversation about electability, and I don’t kind of shy away from those realities."

The progressive congresswoman said of a possible White House run, "I think about it personally."

"I am 36, I’m about to turn 37 years old — and what that means for my life," she added.

AOC, ASKED ABOUT RUNNING FOR PRESIDENT, SAYS HER AMBITION IS 'WAY BIGGER THAN THAT'

"This country has never elected a female president. Why are we pretending that this is not a factor?" she told the Times. "That doesn’t make it impossible, but to act as though it’s not a factor in anything ever is really a form of, like, denialism."

Ocasio-Cortez said the discussion around race and gender was often seen as a complaint or excuse.

"I often hesitate to even talk about it," she told the outlet, "because people then just register it as an excuse or a complaint."

"If you’re asking me about the things that I weigh, of course, that’s part of what I weigh," she told the Times of possibly running for president. "It’s funny because it’s kind of like, everyone else is allowed to talk about it, but I’m not?"

HASAN PIKER BRUSHES OFF DEMS WHO SEE HIM AS A LIABILITY, NAMES HIS '28 CHOICE

She argued people get defensive when gender is suggested as playing a role in electoral politics.

"I experience it tremendously — from the right and from the left," she told the Times.

Ocasio-Cortez has been generating 2028 buzz. LinkedIn co-founder and Democratic megadonor Reid Hoffman described the progressive firebrand as "pragmatic." Hoffman made the comments at Politico's Decoded Summit in September, and said former Vice President Kamala Harris would have a "very challenging path" to the nomination.

"It depends a little bit," Hoffman said when asked whether he would support Ocasio-Cortez for a 2028 run. "I think she's much more pragmatic than people give her credit for."

AOC’S PRIMARY WIN REIGNITES SPECULATION OVER 2028 WHITE HOUSE BID, SCHUMER CHALLENGE

Far-left streamer Hasan Piker said he would absolutely campaign for AOC should she decide to run in 2028.

Ocasio-Cortez topped a July poll from the University of New Hampshire Granite State. In the poll, AOC was one point ahead of former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg and 17 points ahead of Harris.

The polling average as of Sept. 22, according to the New York Times, has Harris leading with 27%, followed by Gov. Gavin Newsom at 16%, Buttigieg with 10%, and Ocasio-Cortez also at 10%.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE OF MEDIA AND CULTURE

Judy Pino, advisor on Hispanic issues and a Spanish-language spokesperson for Independent Women and The LIBRE Initiative, reacted to Ocasio-Cortez' remarks in a statement to Fox News Digital.

Pino said, "Whether America is ready for a Latina president isn’t the question. As a Latina, I find that framing beside the point and, frankly, insulting."

"It reduces a serious debate about the future of this country to gender and ethnicity when Americans are worried about whether they can afford groceries, buy a home, grow a business, and create a better future for their children," she continued.

Pino said Ocasio-Cortez "identifies" with democratic socialism, and argued, "we should believe candidates when they tell us what they stand for."

"For many Latinos, that debate has particular resonance. Families from Cuba, Venezuela and elsewhere in Latin America have witnessed governments embrace socialism while expanding state control and restricting economic and political freedom. Those experiences help explain why the word ‘socialism’ can carry consequences far beyond a political slogan for some Latino families,' Pino said in the statement.

Pino said Latino voters were more focused on AOC's policies rather than her gender or ethnicity.

"That's the debate America should be having: not whether we're ready for a Latina president, but whether Americans want to move this country in a socialist direction," she said.

title: Older women are dying from UTIs. Doctors say a treatment is being missed.
description:
CANTON, Georgia – A nursing home assistant found Roselin Shankland struggling to breathe as she reached Room 204 on her morning rounds.  
Shankland's pulse dropped to 34 beats a minute. Her blood pressure collapsed. 
By the time Shankland reached the hospital the day after Christmas 2023, a urinary tract infection had spread to her bloodstream. Her organs were shutting down.
fullText:
CANTON, Georgia – A nursing home assistant found Roselin Shankland struggling to breathe as she reached Room 204 on her morning rounds.

Shankland's pulse dropped to 34 beats a minute. Her blood pressure collapsed.

Six hours later, the 78-year-old retired nurse was dead.

Her death was the devastating end of a common – and often preventable – health threat facing older women. It also reflected a broader failure to provide menopausal women with a widely recommended treatment that can prevent recurrent urinary tract infections.

Menopause increases the risk of UTIs because declining estrogen changes the tissue and bacteria of the vagina and urinary tract, making it easier for harmful bacteria to grow. In older women, those infections are also more likely to spread to the bloodstream, causing sepsis, organ failure and death.

Vaginal estrogen, a low-dose treatment applied directly to the vaginal tissue as a cream, tablet or ring, can help restore those protections and prevent recurrent infections. It can cost as little as a few dollars a month. Major medical groups have recommended it for years for menopausal women with recurring UTIs, yet many women are never offered it.

Now, a peer-reviewed study of nearly 2 million women with recurrent UTIs provides striking new evidence of its potential benefits. Researchers reviewing medical records from 2017 through 2025 found that women 55 and older who were prescribed vaginal estrogen were about half as likely to be hospitalized with a UTI as those who were not. Their recorded rates of sepsis and death were roughly one-fifth as high.

The study was observational, not a randomized clinical trial, so it cannot prove that vaginal estrogen alone produced those differences — or that the medication would have prevented any individual woman's death. But the findings build upon decades of research showing that vaginal estrogen can reduce recurrent UTIs in menopausal women.

Despite that evidence, only about 1 in 10 menopausal women covered by Medicare uses vaginal estrogen, according to records reviewed by USA TODAY. The treatment remains underused even as UTIs send older women to hospitals and cost Medicare billions of dollars each year.

A misinterpretation of the influential Women's Health Initiative in 2002 prompted the FDA to slap its strongest warning on all estrogen products, including low-dose vaginal estrogen that was never studied in the trial. The sweeping label scared doctors from prescribing medications their patients desperately needed, pushed women off treatment, and contributed to decades of missed opportunities to prevent serious menopause-related health problems for two generations of women we now understand can be fatal.

“This one very simple medicine could have saved my mother,” Shankland’s daughter Lorrie Durbin says. “She spent her life taking care of people. And in the end, no one took care of her. My mother didn’t need to die.”

Now almost one year after the FDA removed the warning label on vaginal estrogen (as well as other estrogen products), its use still isn’t widespread.

Dr. Barry Zisholtz, the senior advisor to the director of the Centers for Disease Control, spent his career prescribing vaginal estrogen to women at his Atlanta area urology practice.

“Every woman in menopause needs vaginal estrogen,” Zisholtz told USA TODAY in an exclusive interview. “Vaginal estrogen prevents women from getting UTIs and keeps women from getting sepsis and out of the hospital. It saves lives.”

USA TODAY interviewed dozens of women who had serious UTIs and their families, physicians and public health officials, and reviewed thousands of pages of these women's medical records to understand this lapse in women’s healthcare and what can be done to help more of them.

Woman after woman told USA TODAY that physicians never talked to their mothers who had become seriously ill or died about vaginal estrogen, something that would have alleviated their painful UTIs – and ultimately prevented them in the first place.

USA TODAY reached out to the FDA for comment. When Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. announced the removal of the warning in fall, he said: “Today, we are standing up for every woman who has symptoms of menopause and is looking to know her options and receive potentially life-changing treatment. For more than two decades, bad science and bureaucratic inertia have resulted in women and physicians having an incomplete view of HRT. We are returning to evidence-based medicine and giving women control over their health again.”

Shankland hit menopause coming off one of the best eras for women’s health care. In the 1990s, hormone replacement therapy was one of the most prescribed medications. More women had access to birth control than ever before. And for the first time, women were included in clinical health trials.

The first Baby Boomers turned 54 in 2000.

Estrogen use plummeted from 27% of menopausal women in 1999 to 5% in 2020, according to the National Institutes of Health.

During a similar period, from 1999 to 2023, women's deaths from sepsis stemming from UTIs nearly tripled for women 45 to 64, according to a USA TODAY analysis of a data from the CDC included in the June 2026 International Journal of Gynecology and Obstetrics.

“This was more than women simply suffering from hot flashes because they weren’t prescribed estrogen. They were dying,” says Dr. Rachel Rubin, a Washington, DC-based urologist and menopause specialist who has studied UTIs and is fellowship trained in sexual medicine. “The lack of implementing guideline-recommended care here is becoming malpractice.”

Shankland raised two girls as a single mother while working full time as a hospital tech and attending night school to become a registered nurse.

She got a job in a Tampa hospital operating room, where Durbin remembers her mother proudly wearing her nurse’s uniform – back when it included a starched hat and white pantyhose. She spent most of her career working for Veterans Affairs hospitals.

“My mother didn’t complain much, but she also was from the generation where you just suffered through it all, sucked it up,” Durbin, 59, says. “This was a woman who worked hard, treated everyone with respect and wouldn’t question doctors.”

When Shankland hit menopause, she was part of a generation that wouldn’t have asked her doctor for hormone replacement therapy, her daughter says. Neither did most women.

“Millions of women stopped getting relief from menopausal symptoms and countless more failed to reap the preventative benefits of menopause hormone therapy,” says Dr. Mary Claire Haver, an obstetrician and gynecologist and certified menopause provider who wrote “The New Menopause.”

Decades later, researchers would say the study had overstated the risk of cancer for younger menopausal women, leading to the FDA removing the black box warning in November 2025.

Even when groups such as the Menopause Society suggested in 2004 that hormone replacement therapy including vaginal estrogen could be used for serious menopause symptoms, the FDA black box warning kept most women from using it.

Shankland and most of her generation complied with the warning and subsequent recommendations from medical groups such as 2005 advice from the AMA Journal of Ethics that women carefully weigh the risks and benefits and that they should use fans or avoid spicy foods that might trigger hot flashes.

But there was something doctors had not told them: Menopausal women are at higher risk for urinary tract infections. And as women get older, these infections can become more dangerous -- even deadly.

As a urologist and professor in Albany, New York, Dr. Elise De, understood the pain her patients faced from UTIs. She also knew that recurring UTIs often became resistant to antibiotics, and she had seen patients die from sepsis.

De led a team of researchers for the June 2026 study in the Urology Journal that became the largest review of its kind. They examined the health records of 1.8 million women with recurring UTIs, and studied the rates of hospital admission, sepsis and death from October 2017 to October 2025. They pulled data from more than 2,070 U.S. hospitals and 47,000 clinics.

The study looked at healthy women as well as those with kidney disease, catheters and diabetes. They looked at women in nursing homes and hospitals and those who simply visited their doctors or urgent care centers. They were particularly interested in menopausal women.

The difference between women who used vaginal estrogen and those who didn’t was striking. In women ages 55 to 69, 1.5% who used vaginal estrogen died versus 7.3% without – almost five times as many. This means vaginal estrogen could have saved the lives of 22,158 women in this age group alone over the eight-year period of the study, according to a USA TODAY analysis of the data.

“No matter their health, menopausal women who were prescribed vaginal estrogen fared better than those who didn’t in everything we studied,” De says. Vaginal estrogen prescriptions in women of any age with recurring UTIs saved lives.

Because this wasn’t a controlled study but rather a review of existing health data, researchers considered which variables they couldn’t measure, such as whether physicians who prescribed vaginal estrogen gave women better care overall.

“It’s hard to argue with this data,” De says. “It’s more than an issue of ‘You can prescribe vaginal estrogen,’ it’s a ‘You should.’ We should have 90% of women 55 and older with UTIs using it.”

The data, she says, points to a system failure, not a patient one.

Judith Lipton spent an entire Saturday afternoon on the couch of her Bellingham, Washington, home in May 2020 when she would usually be riding horses.

It began with a urinary tract infection.

She’d had several UTIs earlier that year, and each time doctors prescribed antibiotics. They never talked to her about prevention.

Lipton spent five days in intensive care.

“I could have died,” Lipton, 75, says now from her home near Santa Barbara, California.

When she saw a new urologist two years ago, he prescribed vaginal estrogen.

“So many of us older ladies don’t know about this. We weren’t on hormones and no one told us we need this,” Lipton says. “I almost died from something that was preventable.”

The week before she planned to visit her in Georgia, Durbin couldn’t reach her mom.

She called Monday and got no answer. She called the next day and left a voicemail.

She texted Shankland’s grandson who had spent part of his summer from New York in Georgia with her. He talked to her every other day. “Have you talked to Grandma?”

Durbin drove straight to Georgia.

Shankland’s front door was unlocked.

She walked through the first floor yelling and found her mother naked on the bedroom floor.

In the emergency room, doctors told Durbin that her mother had a neck fracture and a urinary tract infection.

Shankland was given antibiotics.

Experts say the ER is where critical decisions can be made to help women with chronic UTIs.

UTIs cause some older women to suffer delirium and are often wrongly treated for dementia. Their infections are overlooked. Other times, the delirium from the UTI leads to falls and broken bones.

Dr. Jessica Yearwood, an emergency room physician, noticed more menopausal women with UTIs showing up during her nightshift at a Seattle area urgent care. She and other physicians typically sent them home with antibiotics. These same women would return a few weeks later with another infection.

Yearwood began asking them one question: Are you taking vaginal estrogen?

Yearwood, who also runs her own menopause practice, saw an opportunity to provide the care she saw lacking from many primary care physicians.

Yearwood added a prescription for vaginal estrogen along with antibiotics.

“All of these women were saying, ‘Wow, no one has talked to me about this before,’” she says. “If I’m in a position to help women who might not be getting help from their regular doctors, I’m going to do it. Why would I miss a chance to help these women?”

Shankland spent two weeks in the hospital and was moved to a nursing care center November 13, 2023, to regain her strength.

Admission paperwork noted Shankland was taking eight medications, including a statin, a capsule for constipation, a pain reliever and folic acid. There was no medication listed for UTI prevention. Her crooked signature at the bottom of her admission form stated she wanted doctors to use life-saving measures to keep her alive.

Shankland’s Canton home had been her neighborhood’s gathering place. It had a basement bar and a game room, and she decorated them with wreathes and Santa figurines at Christmastime. Now she struggled to stand on her own or shower independently.

Durbin planned to move her mother down to Tampa with her as Shankland began occupational, physical and speech therapy sessions.

She bought a power lift recliner for her mom to watch reruns of game shows like “The Price is Right” with Shankland’s younger sister, Mary. They two would laugh and bicker so much that Durbin used to joke that she should set up a camera and stream it as a reality show.

Durbin figured the physical therapy would help her mom become strong enough to move home. “It was going to be just six weeks,” she says. “The last time I talked to her, I told her, ‘I love you. We’ve got everything ready for you to come home.’”

Just two weeks after Shankland moved to the care center, her lab results showed a second UTI. A nurse practitioner prescribed five days of antibiotics, taken twice a day until she finished them Dec. 4.

None of Shankland’s doctors ever mentioned that she should be on vaginal estrogen, her daughter says. It was never noted in 830 pages of her care center records that USA TODAY reviewed.

Even now, menopausal women often are only offered vaginal estrogen if they complain of pain during sex. Up to nine in 10 women develop genitourinary syndrome of menopause, which is a collection of symptoms in a woman’s genital tissue and urinary tract caused by low estrogen, according to National Institutes of Health. It leads to incontinence, frequent need to urinate, painful sex and UTIs. All are treated with vaginal estrogen.

Vaginal estrogen can be prescribed several ways, including a twice-weekly cream, inserts or a ring that is inserted every few months for women.

For many years, clinicians blamed women for their own urinary tract infections. They told them to urinate more frequently, to have better hygiene. They never explained that changes in menopausal women’s bodies put them at high risk.

Rubin says UTIs increase with age because of a changing anatomy. Estrogen loss thins the vaginal tissue and changes the microbiome, leading to a less acidic environment -- a breeding ground for harmful bacteria that cause UTIs.  The loss of estrogen starts up to 10 years before a woman begins menopause and lasts the rest of her life, Rubin says.

Systemic estrogen, which menopausal women may be prescribed, often in a patch, can help with bone loss. It does not help prevent UTIs, researchers say. Many medical associations such as the American Urological Association, the Menopause Society and the American College of Obstetricians & Gynecology all recommend vaginal estrogen for menopausal women, especially those with recurring UTIs.

But a generation of physicians who attended medical school during the Women’s Health Initiative were not trained on hormone replacement therapy.

Most doctors – even gynecologists – didn’t receive adequate training in menopause, according to a study in the Journal of The Menopause Society. Less than one-third of the almost 100 obstetrics and gynecology residency program directors recently surveyed said they were taught how to treat menopause symptoms during their residencies.

In reviewing thousands of pages of hospital and nursing home records from women who died from UTIs that turned to sepsis, USA TODAY found one urologist who prescribed a 92-year-old woman with recurring UTIS cranberry supplements in December 2024 instead of vaginal estrogen. She died one month later from sepsis from a UTI.

This education and training gap leaves women without access to experienced menopause providers, a USA TODAY analysis found using data from The Menopause Society. The nonprofit organization provides updated resources and guidelines for health care professionals and certifies providers in menopause care through exams and continuing education.

The USA TODAY analysis shows that there is only one provider who specializes in menopause for every 11,000 women 50 and older in the U.S. There are now almost 6,000 certified menopause care professionals in the United States, most of them physicians. That is up from 1,000 nearly a decade ago, but still far below the number needed to treat all patients.

Amaia Palma, a Realtor in Miami, says no one ever prescribed her mom vaginal estrogen, despite multiple UTIs that caused her to suffer in the last years of her life before dying from Parkinson's disease in 2025.

“She wasn’t having sex, so she didn’t complain. And they didn’t help her,” Palma says. Her mother had been on hormone replacement therapy but stopped taking it in 2003 after doctors told her it was no longer safe.

Palma, 52, met with five doctors before finding one that would prescribe her hormone replacement therapy, including vaginal estrogen.

“I’m just so grateful. I thought I was doomed. I looked at my mom and what she went through, and I didn’t want to be like that,” she says. “We need to take better care of our mothers.”

Durbin’s mother would have turned 81 this year.

When she’s missing her mom, Durbin turns on “MASH,” one of her favorite TV shows. They used to watch it together, her mom pointing out when the show portrayed nurses incorrectly.

She remembers her mother caring for her husband’s ex-wife when she had cancer. “My mom held her hand when she died,” Durbin says.

She also tries hard to forget the morning after Christmas 2023 when a nurse called to tell her that her mom had been found unconscious and was on the way to the hospital.

Shankland was placed on a ventilator.

A nurse practitioner called Durbin that afternoon.

“I told Lori that (her mother) is very sick and from my perspective, she is terminal,” she wrote in Shankland’s hospital report. “(Durbin) said her mom would not want to be kept alive like this. Lori asked me to pray with her mom and make sure that she was not alone. Myself and other nursing staff prayed with (Shankland).”

Shankland was given morphine. A physician noted the time of death: 3:09 p.m.

Durbin hadn’t even started driving to Georgia yet.

“My fear is that she died thinking no one cared,” Durbin said. “She used to tell me was that she was afraid she was going to die alone.”

Durbin’s family has filed a wrongful death lawsuit against the care center. Her lawyer, Michael Hill of Cleveland, Ohio, who specializes in nursing home abuse and neglect, says “vaginal estrogen is the standard of care for these women, and it isn’t provided.”

The company has not returned multiple phone calls and email messages from USA TODAY.

Policy changes, such as improving Medicare’s prescription coverage, could help more women, says Jennifer Weiss-Wolf, executive director of the Birnbaum Women's Leadership Center at New York University.

A three-month supply of generic vaginal estrogen cream through online drug sites, such as Mark Cuban’s Cost Plus, costs $13, rings or inserts, however, can cost up to $1,000 every three months, which can exceed many Medicare plans.

The FDA says that hormone replacement therapy is approved for menopausal symptoms, such as hot flashes and night sweats, and symptoms due to changes to the vagina, vulva, and urinary tract caused by decreased estrogen. Some are approved for osteoporosis. The FDA has retained a warning for endometrial cancer for systemic estrogen products.

It is imperative that women understand vaginal estrogen is safe and necessary, says the CDC’s Zisholtz.

“For 20 years we’ve seen commercials for erectile dysfunction and Viagra,” he says. “We need to take away the embarrassment when talking about women’s health and start saving lives.”

Zisholtz wants to see nursing homes checking if women are on vaginal estrogen upon admission and starting them on prescriptions. He wants menopausal women who are admitted to the hospital for pneumonia, hip surgery or other reasons to be prescribed vaginal estrogen as part of their discharge protocol.

This year’s medical school class will be the first to enter without the FDA warning label on estrogen prescriptions. It might take a generation before those changes are implemented.

“These women, especially my mom’s age, just suffered in silence,” Durbin says. “And now it’s killing them. We need to start treating women like they matter.”

In the past weeks, Durbin had been searching through her Tampa home and storage unit for mementos from her mom, something to remind her of the strong woman who raised two girls alone and later cared for her grandson. The one whose biggest lesson from working at the veteran’s hospital was to treat everyone as if they were important.

Among the items, her Georgia death certificate that states simply: multi-organ failure due to septic shock from a urinary tract infection.

She finds an 8-by-10-inch photo from her mom’s nursing school graduation. Shankland is wearing her starched cap and pressed white uniform dress, holding a red rose.

She can still hear her mother telling her how much everyone matters.

Laura Trujillo is a national columnist focusing on health and wellness. She is the author of "Stepping Back from the Ledge: A Daughter's Search for Truth and Renewal" and can be reached at ltrujillo@usatoday.com.

If you purchase through our links, the USA Today Network may earn a commission. Prices were accurate at the time of publication but may change.

title: ICE officer who shot man in Austin was issued a bodycam but wasn't wearing it
description:
AUSTIN, Texas — The ICE officer who shot a Venezuelan man in Austin on Sunday, leaving a bullet lodged in his back, was issued a body camera but was not wearing it during the shooting, two officials with the Department of Homeland Security told NBC News.
The officials said it was not clear why the officer was not wearing his body camera. Another ICE officer who was in the same vehicle was wearing a body camera, the officials said. That camera captured partial footage of the incident, but the footage does not include the moment of the shooting, the officials said.
Wilber Rafael Garcés Pérez, 28, was shot early Sunday afternoon by an ICE officer while making deliveries as a DoorDash driver.
fullText:
AUSTIN, Texas — The ICE officer who shot a Venezuelan man in Austin on Sunday, leaving a bullet lodged in his back, was issued a body camera but was not wearing it during the shooting, two officials with the Department of Homeland Security told NBC News.

The officials said it was not clear why the officer was not wearing his body camera. Another ICE officer who was in the same vehicle was wearing a body camera, the officials said. That camera captured partial footage of the incident, but the footage does not include the moment of the shooting, the officials said.

Wilber Rafael Garcés Pérez, 28, was shot early Sunday afternoon by an ICE officer while making deliveries as a DoorDash driver. He was taken to a hospital and, four hours after he was shot, was taken into immigration custody at the South Texas ICE Processing Center in Pearsall, Texas, his attorney said. The bullet remains in his back.

On Tuesday, a federal judge granted an emergency order temporarily blocking deportation proceedings against Garcés Pérez, according to his attorney, Kate Lincoln-Goldfinch.

The Travis County District Attorney’s Office also sent a letter to DHS and ICE leadership requesting that Garcés Pérez be allowed to remain in the country since he is “a material witness” in their criminal investigation into the shooting.

Austin Police Chief Lisa Davis shared on Tuesday evening some of the first video footage obtained by the department as part on their probe into the shooting. The videos came from an off-duty officer who captured part of the encounter between ICE and Garcés Pérez, as well as the sound of three gunshots, using his personal dash cam and cellphone.

After this, the off-duty officer alerted his colleagues to the shooting, allowing Austin police to quickly respond to the scene.

Davis said they are seeking the public’s help in obtaining any video evidence that can help them piece together the pursuit that preceded the shooting.

The day after he was shot, Garcés Pérez began “experiencing an inability to move his arm,” attorney Lincoln-Goldfinch said on social media. He was taken to the hospital Monday afternoon for several hours and then sent back to the detention center, she said.

The DHS did not respond to requests for comment about Lincoln-Goldfinch’s statements.

Earlier Monday, Garcés Pérez told a news conference via phone from detention that he was in a lot of pain and wasn’t getting the medical care he needed.

Lincoln-Goldfinch alleged in a social media post that after Garcés Pérez spoke out at the news conference, guards at the detention center “forcibly took the tablet from his hands, revoked his communication privileges, and moved him out of the infirmary into an isolated room with a flat bed that cannot be adjusted like a medical bed.”

He was then taken to the hospital around 5 p.m. after losing his ability to move his arm, she said.

“Wilber reports that he was handcuffed, shackled at the ankles, placed in a waist chain, and handled roughly during that transfer,” she said in the post.

Lincoln-Goldfinch said Garcés Pérez told her on Tuesday morning that doctors spoke to him about his care and gave him morphine for his pain.

“We now understand that the gunshot fractured his clavicle and that he has significant swelling and is wearing a sling,” she wrote. “We still do not have clarity about the cause or extent of the loss of movement he experienced.”

The attorney said Garcés Pérez was discharged from the hospital around midnight and taken back to the detention center, where he is receiving Tylenol and ibuprofen for his ongoing pain.

“He remains in isolation, on a flat bed, and without the tablet he previously used to communicate,” she said.

“We are asking for his communication privileges to be immediately restored and for him to be provided an appropriate medical bed and adequate medical care,” she said. “Most importantly, we are continuing to advocate for Wilber’s IMMEDIATE release.”

Rep. Joaquin Castro, D-Texas, said on social media that “despite losing movement on his left side and having a bullet lodged next to his spine, ICE has forced Wilber Rafael out of the hospital and back to the South Texas ICE Processing Center in Pearsall, Texas.”

He said that he and Rep. Greg Casar, D-Texas, would visit Garcés Pérez on Wednesday, check on his condition and demand his release.

A DHS spokesperson said in a statement late Sunday that Garcés Pérez was in stable condition and was in federal custody pending removal from the U.S.

A senior administration official told NBC News on Monday that Garcés Pérez did not have a criminal history beyond being in the country illegally.

According to Lincoln-Goldfinch, Garcés Pérez entered the country legally and was seeking asylum. She said Garcés Pérez had filed a change of address in immigration court, but received a notice to appear in court at the old address and never got it. Because he missed his immigration hearing, Garcés Pérez was ordered deported in absentia, according to his attorney.

On Monday, Lincoln-Goldfinch shared Garcés Pérez’s account of the shooting, saying he was making a delivery when “an unmarked black truck sideswiped him.” She said he didn’t know it was ICE as the truck chased him as he tried to make a U-turn, and then “pulled him out of the car.”

Previously, DHS has accused immigrants involved in shootings with ICE of using their cars as weapons while fleeing agents, without offering evidence of its claims. But it did not make the accusation in the case of Garcés Pérez or in the case of Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero, who was fatally shot in Biddeford, Maine, in July during a traffic stop.

ICE Director David Venturella previously told NBC News that every ICE officer and agent would be equipped with body cameras by the end of August, adding the agency would allow the “expedited release” of bodycam footage “when appropriate.” Further delaying that timeline is the possibility of DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin potentially switching or adding new vendors for body cameras.

A person who witnessed the aftermath of the shooting but who requested anonymity because he is going through immigration proceedings told Noticias Telemundo that he was waiting on customers at the ice cream shop where he works when he heard gunshots and ran outside, where he saw immigration agents surrounding a car.

“I approached the car and saw a man who looked sad and with his eyes full of tears. I asked him what happened to him, and he just told me, ‘I was shot in the back,’” said the person, a Mexican immigrant who has lived in the U.S. for more than two decades.

“You aren’t prepared to see someone like that. It makes you very angry, it pains you and you don’t know what to do,” he said.

A social media video verified by NBC News captures the sound of tires screeching followed by a person exiting a dark-colored SUV as a blue sedan is stopped next to it, both vehicles facing each other. The sedan appears to be damaged on the passenger side.

At least three gunshots are heard as the person approaches the sedan and runs up to it as it slowly lurches forward. The video shows the person standing next to the sedan’s driver’s side as it stops in front of an intersection.

Another video shows the blue sedan with its driver’s side door open and Garcés Pérez hunched over in the driver’s seat, holding his left upper chest, near his shoulder, as multiple law enforcement officers gather around.

The woman taking the video says, “Why did he do that to him?” The officers tell her that an ambulance is coming.

The video shows Garcés Pérez being taken out of the car and handcuffed behind his back. The agents make him sit on the ground. There appears to be a large bloodstain down his back. The officers cut open the back of his shirt, revealing a bullet hole.

An officer asks the woman taking the video if she saw what happened. In Spanish, she replies that “they just shot him because he didn’t want to stop” his vehicle.

“This is unjust,” she says as she’s recording the video.

Julia Ainsley reported from Washington, D.C., Daniella Silva from New York and Albinson Linares from Austin, Texas.

title: Postal worker told DOJ he tossed 300 mail-in ballots out of 'laziness' and not due to politics
description:
A U.S. postal worker has been charged with throwing away 300 mail-in ballots in Utah. (Patrick T. Fallon / AFP via Getty Images file)
WASHINGTON — An overwhelmed U.
fullText:
WASHINGTON — An overwhelmed U.S. postal worker in Utah threw 300 mail-in ballots into a parking lot dumpster shortly before the state’s June 23 primary election in which both Democrats and Republicans were on the ballot, Justice Department officials said Tuesday.

The 34-year-old mail carrier told investigators that he did not have a political agenda and that he tossed other mail when he ditched the ballots, Melissa Holyoak, U.S. attorney for the District of Utah, said. She said roughly 95% of voters do so by mail in the state, and it wasn’t clear yet whether they were able to eventually cast ballots.

According to a government memo, Damon Matai Seei told investigators that he wanted to toss out advertisements to “lighten his workload” after feeling overwhelmed.

“He claims he simply made a ‘poor decision’ out of ‘frustration’ and ‘laziness,’” the memo said. He didn’t intend to toss any ballots, they said. Seei is no longer with the U.S. Postal Service. He pleaded not guilty Tuesday to a charge of destruction and delay of mail.

Justice Department officials held a news conference in Washington to announce the charge as part of its efforts to promote “election integrity.” Federal prosecutors have made possible voter fraud — which is rare — a priority, as President Donald Trump insists without evidence that noncitizens are voting en masse and has sought to limit mail-in ballots. The Supreme Court last week refused to allow the president’s mail-in restrictions to be enforced.

Trump has repeatedly made false claims that he won the 2020 election and has falsely claimed he won the popular vote in 2016, yet the Trump administration has struggled during both terms to bring cases showing evidence of significant voter fraud. That’s despite a massive effort in Trump’s second term to obtain voter registration records from states in an attempt to determine if there were any noncitizens registered.

So far during the president’s second term, the Justice Department has charged 70 voter-fraud-related cases, officials said Tuesday. More than 170 million people are registered to vote in the U.S.

Acting Deputy Attorney General Trent McCotter said there were more cases in the works, but he didn’t provide further details or a timeline.

“Under the leadership of President Trump and Attorney General Blanche, this department is committed to protecting the vote of American citizens,” he said.

The Justice Department’s Civil Rights Division, meanwhile, is revving up a long-standing election monitoring program but putting a new emphasis on “ballot security” and staffing the effort with newly hired conservative personnel who have replaced longtime career employees, hundreds of whom have departed en masse since Trump returned to office. The Civil Rights Division’s efforts to seize voter rolls have resulted in a string of court losses — with 25 courts ruling against the federal government.

But the materials that the Justice Department releases could help feed Trump’s broader narrative about elections. And with the majority of voters disapproving of Trump’s presidency and saying his policies have hurt the economy, Republicans are facing a tough midterms picture.

Earlier this month, the Justice Department rolled out five voting-related cases, four of which were brought against noncitizens. Last week, the Justice Department announced that 16 individuals had been charged in election-related cases, with a news release mentioning that at least 10 of them were lawful permanent residents of the United States. The defendants were originally from Mexico, Nigeria, India, the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Antigua and Barbuda, Venezuela, and Colombia.

There was also a defendant from Russia: Victoria Aquilina, a 42-year-old Russian national who entered the United States as an au pair in her early 20s, was charged with casting a ballot in the 2024 election.

Trump — who, until he won the 2024 election, faced federal criminal charges over his efforts to overturn his 2020 loss in the lead-up to the Jan. 6, 2021, attack on the Capitol — said earlier this year that Republicans should “nationalize the voting.”

Democrats, meanwhile, have launched an “unprecedented” effort to combat potential disruption of the 2026 midterm elections.

Seei’s next court date is Nov. 30. His federal public defender did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
